Published: 2026-11-14T12:17:42.840

Description:
JSON::XS versions before 4.05 for Perl allow memory exhaustion by buffering incremental input past max_size after a NUL byte in incr_parse.

The parser appends each chunk to its buffer and compares max_size with how far it has progressed, not with the buffer length. It treats a NUL byte as the end of the input, so a NUL within the first max_size bytes keeps it short of the limit. The buffer keeps growing, and incr_skip cannot remove the NUL.

A peer streaming data to an incr_parse consumer can exhaust process memory regardless of max_size.

Text:
Since 2021, Project Zero has followed a “90 + 30” vulnerability disclosure policy, allowing vendors up to 90 days to remediate a vulnerability plus an extra 30 days “soak time” for patch rollout. Our goal was to encourage faster patching and give vendors time to deliver patches to users. The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient.

LLMs have increased the speed at which attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities, alongside the risk that multiple parties, including malicious ones, discover the same bug. A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster.

LLMs have also decreased the time it takes for attackers to reverse engineer and exploit a vulnerability based on a patch, to the extent that zero patch-to-exploitation time is a reasonable, though imperfect, model of attacker behavior. Patch soak time is no longer meaningful in a world where attackers can almost immediately determine bug details from a patch, and can put users at risk by creating a false sense of secrecy. “Patch gap” is the time between a fix being released for a security vulnerability and the user installing the relevant update. It is equally crucial that vendors reduce patch gap, either by reducing patch rollout time or using other strategies to protect users while remediation is in progress.

LLMs have also increased the volume of vulnerabilities that Project Zero reports. We are finding several vulnerabilities a week in targets where we once found a few vulnerabilities a year. Aspects of our policy that require vendor negotiation or agreement, including determining whether a bug is fixed and whether grace period applies, are quickly becoming unmanageable.

Today, we are announcing a new vulnerability disclosure policy, created with the following goals in mind:

- Encourage faster vulnerability remediation
- Encourage vendors to reduce “patch gap”
- Allow for the policy to be automated by both Project Zero and vendors
Title: Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition

Text:
## Our new policy: “Full X”

Vulnerabilities will be disclosed X days after they are reported to the vendor.

Starting today, our policy is “Full 90”, i.e. vulnerabilities will be disclosed 90 days after they are reported to the vendor.

On February 2, 2027, we will move to a “Full 60” policy where vulnerabilities are disclosed after 60 days.

On January 3, 2028, we will move to a “Full 30” policy where vulnerabilities are disclosed after 30 days.

We are also removing most ‘special cases’ from our disclosure policy, including grace period and variant policy. The only exceptions to our new policy are:

- Vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild -- ITW vulnerabilities will be handled according to Google’s [application security vulnerability disclosure policy](https://about.google/company-info/appsecurity/)
- Public vulnerabilities -- Project Zero may make details of a vulnerability public, at our discretion, if the details have already been made public by others
- Vendor request -- We will make vulnerability details public if the vendor we reported it to requests it

### Why reduce remediation time gradually?

Project Zero solicited feedback from the vendors we report the most vulnerabilities to as a part of developing this new policy. An overarching concern was that immediately changing the policy could harm users by making unfixed vulnerabilities available to attackers while vendors are in the process of improving their remediation processes and technology. While the benefits of delaying disclosure are declining due to the increased probability that attackers will discover a vulnerability during the embargo period, we still feel there are benefits in the short term.

In addition, vendors mentioned two more subtle concerns. One was that an overly-aggressive disclosure policy would encourage fixing bugs reported under the new policy with more priority, even if they are less severe than other reported vulnerabilities. The other was that immediately enforcing a policy that some vendors aren’t equipped to meet might lead to a state where vendors accept that they cannot fix bugs within the deadline and don’t attempt to.

We decided on a policy that encourages vendors to improve remediation time on a schedule that is challenging but realistic, with the hope that this will lead to vendors broadly improving their remediation processes and infrastructure in a way that eventually enables them to fix all reported vulnerabilities quickly.
Title: Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition

Text:
### What about severity?

While our analysis isn’t always perfect, Project Zero only reports vulnerabilities with substantial severity and demonstrated security impact in our tracker. That said, we don’t feel severity is an effective metric for making disclosure decisions, especially in the current environment. A vulnerability’s severity does not affect the likelihood that it will be discovered by attackers, only its impact on users.

When vendors determine severity and use it to prioritize bug fixes, they are making decisions about what risks they are willing to expose their users to, and it is reasonable to accept the risk of low-severity bugs, like unexploitable null pointer crashes or minor info leaks in a lot of circumstances. But this doesn’t change the availability of these vulnerabilities to attackers, and we want our policy to reflect this reality.

It’s also important to acknowledge that Project Zero holds itself to high standards with regards to the reproducibility, readability, reachability and reported security impact of the vulnerabilities we report. This policy assumes bugs reports are of this quality, and it is reasonable for vendors to treat low quality-bug reports differently.

### What about hardware?

We encourage all vendors to consider how they would respond to imminent disclosure of a serious vulnerability, including non-patch [strategies](https://projectzero.google/2026/10/emergency-patching.html), as there is no guarantee that defenders will be the first to find a bug. That said, Project Zero has occasionally granted [exceptions](https://projectzero.google/vulnerability-disclosure-faq.html#exceptions) to our policy on rare occasions, including Spectre and Meltdown, and will continue to do so in the future.

### Are you really not going to check whether bugs are fixed?

The question of whether a bug is fixed for the purposes of our policy has always been challenging and somewhat unresolved, particularly with regards to code that is not shipped directly to users and not publicly available. It is not unusual for Project Zero to communicate with vendors multiple times for each bug report to come to an agreement on whether a vulnerability is fixed. As more vendors experiment with vulnerability remediation strategies that are not patching like temporarily disabling code paths, we expect this to become even more complex.
Title: Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition

Text:
### Are you really not going to check whether bugs are fixed?

We still plan to track whether bugs are fixed and communicate if they are not, however, this will not be a decision point in our policy. This will enable us to share technical details of how users are protected without needing to make a binary judgement with consequences for the vendor.
Title: Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition

Text:
## Summary

Project Zero compared two automated tools used by Google to find vulnerabilities in Chrome’s JavaScript engine, V8, on a regular basis. [Fuzzilli](https://github.com/googleprojectzero/fuzzilli) is a generative JavaScript engine fuzzer and [BigSleep](https://projectzero.google/2024/10/from-naptime-to-big-sleep.html) is an LLM-based bug finding system. In the past six months, BigSleep found more vulnerabilities than Fuzzilli (45 versus 37) with a 25% overlap in the specific bugs reported. Since this comparison methodology has a tendency to underestimate overlap, we also performed dedicated experiments to test theoretical overlap in vulnerabilities reported since 2023. These experiments estimated overlap at roughly 60%. Regardless of which value is accurate, a substantial portion of vulnerabilities were discoverable by only LLMs or only fuzzing. While it is extremely promising that LLMs have become able to find so many vulnerabilities so quickly, fuzzing and LLMs are still complementary approaches. We recommend vendors perform both fuzzing and agentic analysis of their code to maximize the number of vulnerabilities that get reported before they impact users.
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

Text:
## Introduction

Fuzzing has long been successfully applied to software projects such as Chrome or V8 (Chrome’s JavaScript engine) to detect bugs. Recently, the arrival of powerful LLMs able to read, reason about, and write code is causing a transformative change to software development and software security. With [hundreds, sometimes thousands of new bugs and vulnerabilities](https://blog.google/security/chrome-stronger-with-every-update/) having been discovered in well-fuzzed targets, a natural question arises: how do new LLMs compare to “traditional” fuzzers? Are they starting to replace them or do the two approaches complement each other? To help answer this, we look at three key questions:

1. How many bugs does each approach find in the real world?
2. What is the overlap between the two approaches?
3. What is the “shape” of bugs discovered by one system but not the other?

For this blog post, we will limit ourselves to two concrete systems: [Fuzzilli](https://github.com/googleprojectzero/fuzzilli), a JavaScript engine fuzzer, and [BigSleep](https://projectzero.google/2024/10/from-naptime-to-big-sleep.html), an agentic bug finding system. Both of these systems run in production and automatically look for bugs in newly added code, which makes them fairly directly comparable. Specifically, Fuzzilli runs continuously across many instances, with the first ones usually picking up new changes within a few hours, while BigSleep currently runs once per day and is prompted to review new commits and write proof-of-concept testcases for any bugs it discovers. Both systems report bugs through [Clusterfuzz](https://github.com/google/clusterfuzz), which will do basic crash triaging, then file bug reports in [Chrome’s issue tracker.](https://issues.chromium.org/home)

We also limit ourselves to V8 as a target, a high-performance JavaScript and WebAssembly engine with a sophisticated and mature testing and fuzzing setup. In particular, Fuzzilli is a special-purpose fuzzing tool designed to find bugs in these engines. The usually complicated nature of these bugs makes for an interesting “playground” to compare the two approaches’ ability to find deep and complex bugs in well-tested software. We leave it to future work to perform similar analysis on a broader set of targets, fuzzers, and agentic bug finding systems.
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

Text:
## Introduction

We will now look into each of the three main questions in a dedicated section. Each section will first summarize the general approach, then describe the methodology in detail (often as bullet points, so you can skip those blocks if you don’t care too much about the details) before exploring the results. We conclude with an attempt at interpreting the results to get a picture of the current state of fuzzing vs. AI.
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

Text:
# Part 1: Production Statistics

This is the simplest part to analyze, although with some caveats we’ll see in a bit. The basic idea is to query issues from [Chromium’s bugtracker](http://issues.chromium.org/) (where V8 bugs are tracked) and extract various statistics from there. This is especially easy since there’s a dedicated hotlist for each of the two systems. We limit our analysis to the six months from April to September 2026 as the automatic BigSleep pipeline only became active in April this year. As such, our raw data comes from the following two bug tracker queries:

- Fuzzilli: [hotlistid:5433121 created:2026-04-01..2026-09-30](https://issues.chromium.org/issues?q=hotlistid:5433121%20created:2026-04-01..2026-09-30)
- BigSleep: [hotlistid:8067258 created:2026-04-01..2026-09-30](https://issues.chromium.org/issues?q=hotlistid:8067258%20created:2026-04-01..2026-09-30)

From there, the raw numbers of bug reports are:

- Fuzzilli: 316
- BigSleep: 441

Small win for BigSleep. However, this includes all types of bugs, and BigSleep initially also found a lot of configuration and integration issues in V8, for example [crbug.com/503869331](https://crbug.com/503869331) where the [unsafe flag blocking mechanism](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:v8/src/flags/flag-definitions.h;l=4303;drc=4bd243831302ef96b70f7e159e5685bb2eba306f) didn’t work properly yet. These are legitimate issues, but less relevant for our comparison since there’s little real-world security impact. One easy way to get rid of these is to look specifically at vulnerabilities by limiting the results to `type:vulnerability`:

- Fuzzilli: 178
- BigSleep: 95

Suddenly a clear win for the fuzzers? Not quite. There are still some problems with this data, notably duplicates and unactionable reports (e.g. bugs [closed as WAI](https://issues.chromium.org/issues?q=hotlistid:\(8067258%20%7C%205433121\)%20status:intended_behavior)). At first, this seems like a simple thing to fix: just include another constraint such as `status:(fixed | verified)`. Unfortunately, things are a bit more complicated. Take for example Fuzzilli bug [crbug.com/511935486](https://crbug.com/511935486). The events on this bug are basically:

- The bug is filed by Clusterfuzz on May 11 and assigned to an engineer
- The bug is closed by Clusterfuzz as the testcase no longer reproduces later that same day
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

# Part 1: Production Statistics

As such, this bug received zero developer interactions. Most likely what happened here is that this bug was a duplicate of another bug, [crbug.com/511210507](https://crbug.com/511210507), but Clusterfuzz didn’t realize it as the crash signature (derived from the stack trace) was slightly different. When the other bug received a fix, the testcase stopped reproducing on Clusterfuzz, which closed the issue.

Maybe the best thing we can do is to look at “actionable” bugs, defined as those that are not marked as duplicates or WAI and that received at least one fix commit referencing them. Then, looking at only `Type-Vuln` bugs filters out a lot of the less-relevant BigSleep bugs, even though these were “actionable”. With that, the final picture looks like this:

So in terms of vulnerabilities, it’s roughly a tie (small advantage BigSleep) at the moment: 45 vs. 37.

This naturally raises the question of cost: how expensive is each of the two approaches and what does that mean in terms of cost-per-bug? Unfortunately, it’s challenging to make a comparison at this stage in the research. While some effort has been dedicated to making Clusterfuzz more efficient, similar effort has not been expended for Big Sleep and neither system is particularly calibrated for an optimal cost-per-bug ratio.
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

Text:
# Part 2: Overlap

The next question is how much these approaches overlap each other. For this, our approach is twofold: we first attempt to find an answer in the bugtracker, by trying to identify bugs discovered by both systems. Next, we run a dedicated experiment in which we let BigSleep try to rediscover old Fuzzilli bugs.

## Bugtracker Overlap

The basic idea is to see which bugs were found by both systems, so we’re effectively looking for duplicate bug reports. Similar to part 1, there are a few steps we need to take to ensure we get a somewhat accurate picture:

- First, we look for bugs filed by one system that get deduplicated into a bug filed by the other. For example [crbug.com/522410841](https://crbug.com/522410841) which is a duplicate of [crbug.com/522860268](https://crbug.com/522860268). This is a clear overlap.
- Next, we need to take into account that many “unactionable” reports (those with zero associated fixes) are often duplicates. For those reports, we need to find the commit that fixed them, then look at the bug associated with that commit, and treat these two bugs as duplicates. This can be a multi-prong relationship: both bug X found by BigSleep and bug Y found by Fuzzilli might be a duplicate of bug Z reported by someone/something else. In that case, that bug still counts as overlap.
- Then, we need to realize that many duplicates never receive a bugtracker entry since they are already deduplicated at the Clusterfuzz level (since both Fuzzilli and BigSleep rely on Clusterfuzz for basic triage and bug filing). As such, we need to query Clusterfuzz’s underlying database to find more duplicates.
- Finally, we need to decide what to do with separate bugs that get fixed by the same CL, for example the four bugs fixed by [crrev.com/c/7965120](https://crrev.com/c/7965120). While this can legitimately happen for distinct bugs, it’s probably more likely for the bugs to be duplicates (such as in this case), and so we count them as such.

With all the different types of deduplication, we get this final picture:

Again, looking at just the actionable vulnerability reports (likely the best measure), we see an overlap of roughly 25% (20 out of a total of 81), with a slight majority of these found first by Fuzzilli and later by BigSleep.
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

Text:
## Overlap Experiment

The second way to measure the overlap is to run a dedicated experiment in which we try to re-discover bugs found by one system in the past using the other. Specifically, here we try to re-discover old Fuzzilli bugs using a BigSleep setup that’s as close to the production configuration as possible. For each bug we collect the commit that (likely) introduced the bug, and ask the agent to review those changes just as in the production CI environment. Note that the other direction, trying to rediscover past BigSleep bugs with Fuzzilli is more difficult to set up, since fuzzers cannot easily be given a similar “starting point”. Moreover, for many of these bugs we already know the outcome of such an experiment: the majority of “historic” BigSleep bugs (e.g. [those from 2025](https://issues.chromium.org/issues?q=hotlistid:8067258%20componentid:1456824%2B%20created%3C2026-01-01)) were found after fuzzers like Fuzzilli had already been fuzzing vulnerable builds for months, sometimes years. So they would most likely also not rediscover them in an experiment (except perhaps in a few cases where Fuzzilli was since updated to support new language features). Similarly, in production, BigSleep only reports crashes with a delay of 1-2 days (as there’s currently only one run per day). As such, fuzzers also get a head-start there.

In more detail, here is how the experiment is set up:
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

Text:
## Overlap Experiment

- We start with a list of historic Fuzzilli bugs (from early 2023 until mid-2026) by querying the bug tracker hotlist. This gives us [around 1150 raw bugs](https://issues.chromium.org/issues?q=hotlistid:5433121%20status:\(fixed%20%7C%20verified\)%20created%3C2026-08-01).
- We restrict this to only `type:vulnerability` as these are the types of bugs we care most about and will remove some “noise” as above. We are left with roughly 600 vulnerabilities.
- Next, we filter this list down to bugs that reproduce in the environment used by the agent. This involves two parts:
  - Bugs that reproduce on an x64 debug+asan build of the d8 shell as [provided by Chrome’s public build infrastructure](https://commondatastorage.googleapis.com/v8-asan/index.html?prefix=linux-debug/). This is important because many bugs only reproduce in special builds, for example because they are architecture-specific or need certain compile-time features.
  - Bugs that can be reproduced without special flags. The problem here is that fuzzers often set custom flags, either to enable in-development features (e.g. `--experimental-wasm-jspi` in [crbug.com/361123483](http://crbug.com/361123483)) or to turn on different fuzzing modes that make certain types of bugs easier to discover (e.g. `--deopt-every-n-times` in [crbug.com/362784006](https://crbug.com/362784006)). However, we can’t let the agent set arbitrary flags on historic V8 builds as these didn’t have a “safe-flags only” mode (leading to many false-positive crashes), and we also don’t want to tell the agent which flags it should use for a given challenge as that would be a hint. As such, for simplicity we limit ourselves to bugs that can reproduce with a standard set of flags (`--fuzzing`, `--jit-fuzzing`, `--expose-gc`) and only allow the agent to set those.
- We end up with 132 historic bugs.
- We now perform some deduplication similar to what we did above to identify implicit duplicates, which we remove. This leaves us with a final number of 112 bugs.
- For a realistic comparison, we then convert these bugs into “code review challenges” similar to the ones used by the production BigSleep pipeline. For that, we try to identify the commit that (likely) introduced the bug, for example based on bisection. We note that this skews the comparison against BigSleep for two reasons:
  - We likely sometimes identify the wrong commit that is unrelated to the bug in question, making the task harder or even impossible.
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

Text:
## Overlap Experiment

  - We only have one commit per bug, while in the real world, the agent might discover the bug from another, subsequent commit that touches a similar part of the codebase.
- We now run the agent for 25 attempts on each commit. The agent is asked to find bugs related to the commit and prove their existence by writing a testcase that crashes the vulnerable build. The attempt is terminated once a crash is found, so each attempt can report at most one bug. We use essentially the same configuration that was used in production BigSleep at that time, including the same underlying model: [Gemini 3.6 flash](https://deepmind.google/models/model-cards/gemini-3-6-flash).
- Finally, we run some post-processing on the results to check if the agent found the “right” bug or an unrelated one. For that, we check that the testcase crashes the pre-fix revision but not the post-fix revision. This is imperfect but fairly easy to implement.

Here are the results from the experiment:

Starting from just the commits that (likely) introduced the bugs, BigSleep was able to re-discover ~62% of the original bugs, while finding a different (but by now fixed) bug for another ~12% of commits. On around 26% of the commits it failed to find any bugs.

### Memorization

One thing to worry about with experiments such as this one is memorization: the LLM remembering specific bugs from its (pre-)training data and as such having an easier time “re-discovering” them during evaluation. We can try to get some idea of the effect of this by looking at the success rates for bugs from different time spans, e.g. every half-year period for which we have bugs in the data set. If there was memorization, we’d expect higher success rates (both for a single attempt and for the combined run) on bugs prior to the learning data cutoff of the model. Here are the results for our experiment:
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

Text:
### Memorization

For the model used in this experiment (Gemini 3.6 flash), the [knowledge cutoff date is March 2026](https://deepmind.google/models/model-cards/gemini-3-6-flash/#intended-usage-and-limitations). Combining that with the fact that in early 2026, Chrome bugs would only become publicly visible after ~3 months, the effective knowledge cutoff for Fuzzilli bugs should be around Jan 2026. Looking at the data, there seems to be no statistically significant amount of memorization pre-2026. We note, however, that this may be different for other models or future model generations and as such recommend that this be re-evaluated for similar experiments in the future.

### Difficulty

A follow-up question we might ask is how the overlap compares with “difficulty”. For example, in the best case a system like BigSleep would easily find issues that fuzzers struggle with and vice versa. In that case, budget that was previously spent on long fuzzing sessions may now be re-allocated and put to different uses. Here are the results of analysing this, where “bug difficulty” is measured by the time it took Fuzzilli to discover the bug:

While we do get a statistically significant result here (although not of particularly great magnitude), it actually points in the other direction! Bugs that are hard to find for a fuzzer are likely also hard to find for an AI agent. As such, those fuzzers should probably be kept running for now.

### Components

Another thing we can look at is a per-component breakdown of the bugs and their rediscovery rates:

Interestingly, the overlap is significantly smaller for compiler bugs. This is the area where Fuzzilli probably specializes most in, which may explain the results. Later on (in part 3), we’ll also develop another hypothesis for why (some) bugs in the compilers may be more difficult to rediscover for BigSleep.

### Prompting

A final question is how much the specific prompting played a role in the performance of the AI agent. For that, we run two quick follow-up experiments, only on the bugs that weren’t previously re-discovered and with different prompts:
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

Text:
### Prompting

1. Instead of starting from commits, we start from the vulnerable file or function. This may be an easier starting point but is still a fairly realistic setup since both can for example be obtained by extracting modified files and functions from a given commit.
2. Instead of asking the agent to find memory corruption vulnerabilities (what we care most about), we specifically tell it that assertion failures and similar crashes are also desirable.

Running these two experiments with only 5 attempts per bug (instead of the 25 used in the main experiment), the agent re-discovered 10 additional bugs in total: 8 from the different starting points and 7 with the rephrased prompt (with 5 found in both runs).

In total, combining these results with our original experiment, we get the following picture:

So the share of “correct” bugs found climbs to ~70%, and we find some kind of bug for ~84% of starting points. However, for fairness it should be noted that equivalent tweaks to a fuzzer could likely also result in higher discovery rates for certain bugs, so the results of this follow-up experiment should be treated with some caution.
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

Text:
## Summary

The main results from our two angles are:

1. In production, the overlap is noticeable but not substantial at around 25%.
2. In our experiment, overlap was around 60% of historic Fuzzilli bugs (70% with additional runs that used different prompts).
3. The overlap is not uniformly distributed:
  1. Bugs that are difficult for a fuzzer to find are more likely to also be difficult to find for an agent, so there’s more overlap on “easy” bugs.
  2. The overlap seems to be smaller in the JIT Compilers and higher in the rest of the engine.

From just the experiment, we might expect a higher overlap in production. However, there are probably a few factors that prevent(ed) this:

- There’s a limited time window for overlaps: once a bug reported by either system is fixed, the other system no longer has a chance to rediscover it (as the bug won’t reproduce on Clusterfuzz and will therefore be discarded).
- Our experiment only looked at a subset of Fuzzilli bugs that reproduce on a standard x64 d8 fuzzer build and without special flags. In production, each system has access to slightly different and specialized builds, as well as different runtime flag constraints, and there the overlap is potentially smaller.
- Pipeline hiccups such as overloaded servers or bugs in the automation likely prevented a number of commits from being reviewed by BigSleep in the last months, so bugs introduced by them may have been missed.
- Since its introduction in April, the model underlying the BigSleep pipeline has been upgraded multiple times. Earlier models likely performed worse, and we expect future models to perform better.
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

# Part 3: Shape of Bugs

In this section, we will first look at three case studies of bugs found by one system but not the other, then attempt to draw conclusions from these and other bugs.

## BigSleep: Chrome Bug 449760249 (October 2025)

This [bug](https://crbug.com/449760249) is a nice example of BigSleep benefiting from the underlying model’s reasoning capabilities to discover a variant that was (likely) too complex to trigger by a fuzzer in a reasonable amount of time. It’s also a good example to show the general working of an agentic bug finding system.

### Background: TDZ and Hole Check Elision

Before diving into the bug specifics, we first need to look at some JavaScript internals, specifically variable initialization. In JavaScript, variables declared with the `let` or `const` keywords cannot be used before they are initialized, and attempting to do so will lead to an exception (`”ReferenceError: Cannot access 'foobar' before initialization”`). In V8’s terminology, these variables reside in a “temporal dead zone” (TDZ) until they are initialized. Internally, V8 sets variables in the TDZ to a special sentinel value, `the_hole`, and then checks for this value when accessing the variable’s content.

To limit the performance impact of these hole-checks, V8’s bytecode compiler implements an optimization (behind the [default-enabled --ignition-elide-redundant-tdz-checks flag](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:v8/src/flags/flag-definitions.h;l=1215;drc=424b93eb76684237b932b5d79315d00b85297548)) to identify redundant checks and subsequently remove them. The idea here is to identify “dominating” checks where it can then be guaranteed that a hole-check has already been performed for a given variable on all possible paths leading to the current position.

This is a security-relevant optimization as an incorrectly removed hole-check would result in the internal `the_hole` value leaking to JavaScript code, a condition that [has historically been exploitable](https://crbug.com/40057710) (although [new mitigations](https://crbug.com/434179415) for this bug class have since shipped).
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

Text:
### The Original Vulnerability

The original bug ([issue 40071027](https://crbug.com/40071027) - discovered two years earlier by Fuzzilli!) involved `do-while` loops containing a `break` statement. In a `do-while` loop, the loop condition evaluates after the body. If the condition contains an assignment to a variable, the bytecode compiler will mark the variable as initialized. However, if a `break` statement executes in the loop body in the first iteration, then the condition will never execute. The bytecode compiler originally failed to account for this, leading to an incorrectly omitted hole check and subsequent leak of `the_hole` value.

Specifically, the patch works by creating a [`HoleCheckElisionScope`](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:v8/src/interpreter/bytecode-generator.cc;l=445;drc=7a23bdae2d6c30b956f4f5803e3b7431a6632667) for processing the condition code in case the loop contains break statements. This means that any updates to the TDZ state of variables will be discarded once the scope object is destroyed. As such, code after the loop will see the previous TDZ state (which is the correct behavior in this case).

### Discovery of the Variant

The BigSleep agent began its analysis by examining the patch to `VisitDoWhileStatement`, realizing that the fix relied on `loop_builder.break_labels()->empty()` to decide if a protective `HoleCheckElisionScope` was required. It then began creating and testing various hypotheses for scenarios in which no `break` statement was registered with a given loop but the condition would still be skipped at runtime. For example, it hypothesized that a try-catch in combination with a `throw` inside the loop might confuse the hole-check elision logic. It then investigated how try-catch was implemented in the bytecode compiler and concluded that this was handled correctly.

Eventually, the agent started investigating [labeled breaks](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/label), which allow directly breaking out of inner loops. It hypothesized that these might not be handled correctly and continued to investigate how these were being processed, for example by studying the logic in `BytecodeGenerator::VisitBreakStatement`. This time, it seemed to have identified a real flaw: in the case of nested breaks, the inner loop was apparently not being informed of the existence of a break statement! It therefore formulated the following vulnerability hypothesis:
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

Text:
### Discovery of the Variant

1. If a labeled break inside a `do-while` loop targets an outer scope, the inner `do-while` loop’s `LoopBuilder` is not notified.
2. Consequently, `loop_builder.break_labels()->empty()` remains `true`.
3. Therefore, when generating the code for the loop condition, the `HoleCheckElisionScope` introduced by the patch is not used.
4. The condition is bypassed at runtime, but the bytecode compiler erroneously removed a later hole-check, leading to a leak of `the_hole` to JavaScript.

The agent then began writing a testcase to prove the existence of this bug. The initial attempt with simply two nested loops and a label failed, however, as the bytecode compiler would [add another protective scope object for the labeled block](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:v8/src/interpreter/bytecode-generator.cc;l=2099;drc=77ce2c33f61b01daac3d9e4299b3d0805bee6461). To work around this, the agent decided to use a `switch` statement. When handling a `switch` statement, the bytecode compiler uses a `HoleCheckElisionMergeScope` to compute the intersection of initialization states across all branches. By ensuring that the variable was initialized in a `default` case, the merge logic then concluded that the variable was correctly initialized on all paths.
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

## BigSleep: Chrome Bug 443765373 (September 2025)

This [bug](https://crbug.com/443765373) is an example of a relatively simple bug type that is challenging to discover with standard fuzzing approaches.

### Background: Exception handling in V8

For the purpose of this bug, the relevant part is mostly the last line of the output. Here, the bytecode essentially says “if there is an exception while the PC is between offset 3 and 6 in this bytecode, then execution should continue at offset 6 (the start of the exception handler)”.

### The Bug

Such a testcase would again be difficult to craft by a fuzzer as the fuzzer isn’t rewarded for creating large code (at least not with generic coverage feedback). In fact, the fuzzer is likely even actively discouraged from finding this bug since generating and executing large bytecode takes some time (in debug builds, the testcase generated by the agent needs a few seconds to trigger) and would therefore probably have led to timeouts during fuzzing.
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

Text:
## Fuzzilli: Chrome Bug 40076141 (November 2023)

This [bug](https://crbug.com/40076141) is a good example of a type of bug that is likely difficult to find just by looking at (one part) of the source code. It was originally discovered by Fuzzilli and not rediscovered by any of the experiments from part 2.

### Background: Value Representation in V8

Here we create multiple variables holding values of different types. Note, however, that we never declare the type of a variable, and that variables can hold values of different types throughout their lifetime (`i` first contains an integer, later a string). What we see here is that JavaScript is a dynamically typed language, and so variables (and also object fields, etc.) have no fixed type. However, the actual runtime values still need to have a type: the engine somehow needs to know that `foobar` is a string value and that certain operations (e.g. substring search) can therefore be performed on it. Conceptually, this is possible by representing runtime values with a struct such as

However, this is somewhat inefficient since we now need something like 16 bytes to represent a simple 4-byte integer at runtime. As such, modern JS engines use clever tagging schemas, which rely on unused pointer bits to encode type information. Specifically, in V8 the `JSValue` type is a tagged pointer (or just `tagged` for short) which stores one bit of type information in the least-significant bit:

- If the bit is one, then the value minus 1 is a pointer to another object. This works because objects are aligned and so cannot start at an uneven address.
- If the bit is zero, then the next 31 bits contain a raw integer value (also called a small integer - Smi)

As such, to figure out the type of a value at runtime, the engine first looks at the least-significant bit. If that is zero, the value can be “untagged” to obtain the integer value by right-shifting by one. On the other hand, if the bit is one, the value is a valid pointer to an object that contains further type information. For more details on V8’s pointer tagging scheme see also [this blog post](https://v8.dev/blog/pointer-compression#value-tagging-in-v8).

### The Testcase

The bug is caused during optimization of the loop by the Maglev compiler, specifically due to a conflict between two stages of the compiler pipeline: the initial graph builder and the later MaglevPhiRepresentationSelector.
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

Text:
### The Graph Builder

The graph builder is responsible for building the initial Maglev intermediate representation (IR) of the code. For that, it consumes both the input code (in the form of V8 bytecode) as well as runtime feedback that was collected while the code executed in lower tiers such as the interpreter. When processing the loop in this testcase, the following happens:

1. Both `i3` and `v2` are modified during the loop. Since the IR uses [static single-assignment (SSA) form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Static_single-assignment_form), these turn into Phi nodes, which make the code look like every variable only has a single assignment :)
2. For the `i3 >= v2` comparison, the runtime feedback states that `i3` was so far always a Smi and therefore speculates that this will be the case in the future. It guards this assumption by emitting a `CheckedSmiUntag`, which will extract the raw int from the tagged value and will bail out to the interpreter if the input is ever not a Smi.
3. For the following operations on `v2`, the compiler can then rely on the existing check and emit `UnsafeSmiUntag` nodes, which avoid the runtime checks but are only safe to use if the input is guaranteed to be a Smi.

### The Conflict

The bug now occurs because of two optimizations interacting badly with each other:

1. The graph builder uses `UnsafeSmiUntag` as it believes that the value must be a Smi at this point
2. The representation selector removes a `CheckedSmiUntag` as it believes it is no longer required

Specifically, what can happen now is that eventually, `i3` becomes larger than the maximum Smi value. At that point, `Int32ToNumber` can no longer fit the integer into a `Smi` and instead allocates a `HeapNumber` object (a container holding a larger number, basically). At this point, however, the `UnsafeSmiUntag` is no longer safe as the input is now a pointer. This leads to a corrupted pointer value being extracted and subsequently to memory corruption. Note that in the original code, this could not have happened as the `HeapNumber` would’ve been rejected by the `CheckedSmiUntag(i3)`.

What may have made this bug difficult to find for BigSleep is the fact that both optimizations are correct in isolation. As such, looking at just one of them would’ve made it difficult to spot the issue. The agent would somehow have needed to hypothesize about the other optimization or stumbled upon the relevant code by chance (or exhaustive search).
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

Text:
## Overview

Looking at the examples above as well as other bugs found by LLMs, we can see a few clear examples of bugs where an LLM has the advantage:

- Bugs that require complex logic to trigger but can be found through progressive logical reasoning and experimentation with the target program, such as [crbug.com/449760249](http://crbug.com/449760249) discussed above. This is likely the strongest advantage.
- Bugs that require specific “magic” values (e.g. edge-case integers, specific strings, etc.), such as [crbug.com/443765373](https://crbug.com/443765373) discussed above.
- Bugs that require new (or less common) features that a fuzzer may not be aware of. Examples include [crbug.com/436181695](https://crbug.com/436181695), where the fuzzer didn’t support the new `await using` syntax yet, and in fact also [crbug.com/449760249](http://crbug.com/449760249) above where Fuzzilli lacked support for labeled breaks at the time.
- Bugs that require a non-standard harness, custom flags, or special helper tools/functions that a fuzzer is not configured to use (e.g. [crbug.com/516833326](https://crbug.com/516833326) which required --expose-fast-api and the `d8.test.FastCAPI` API).

On the other hand, here are some advantages that fuzzers enjoy (for now):
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

Text:
## Overview

- They can find “non-local” bugs reasonably well if not too many individual pieces are required. [crbug.com/40076141](http://crbug.com/40076141) discussed above is an example for such a bug.
- They can find bugs that are hard to spot by reasoning about the source code alone. One clear example would be bugs caused by (incorrect) C++ compiler optimizations such as [crbug.com/500771385](https://crbug.com/500771385). Another potential example is bugs such as [crbug.com/414840455](https://crbug.com/414840455), which are related to handling dead code in V8’s compilers. This is likely an unusual state and therefore may be hard to reason about. BigSleep missed a few of these in our experiments.
- They are immune to certain biases affecting the agentic approaches, such as the choice of starting point (e.g. commits), the exact prompt phrasing, or the bug types seen (and not seen) during training. They do suffer from other types of biases though (e.g. the weights of individual mutators and generators).
- They don’t get distracted by “shallow” bugs, whereas BigSleep missed a few bugs because it found easier ones instead. This is probably somewhat self-correcting though as the shallow bugs would eventually get fixed, giving the agent another chance to discover the deeper bug.

There is probably also a category of bugs that are hard to find for both approaches: bugs that are very non-local (bad for the agent) and require complex testcases (bad for the fuzzer) to trigger. In this case, a fuzzer would probably discover the individual pieces of the testcase (through coverage feedback) but won’t be able to find the right combination to trigger the bug (as in our first example). A code-reviewing agent, on the other hand, may struggle with the large search space of code fragments that may interact badly with each other (as in our last example). This is only a hypothesis, however, and would require further experiments and data to validate.
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

Text:
# Part 4: Conclusion

In this blog post, we’ve compared coverage-guided fuzzers with vulnerability-discovery agents that read and reason about the source code. Specifically, we’ve looked at Fuzzilli and BigSleep, which both run as automated pipelines on V8 to discover newly introduced bugs. Looking at the data from those pipelines, we saw a roughly equal share of vulnerabilities found in the last 6 months (around 40 each), and a moderate overlap in discovered bugs of around 25%. However, in a dedicated experiment, overlap was closer to 60%. For now, this means that the two approaches remain complementary, and specialized fuzzing continues to provide value by finding bugs quickly and identifying certain kinds of issues that are otherwise hard to spot. At the same time, LLMs only very recently became capable of finding bugs in software like V8 at all, and have made tremendous progress since. The model used for our experiment is by now already outdated and outperformed by newer generations. Looking to the future, we expect further model improvements, potentially coupled with better prompting and more flexible harnesses (that e.g. allow the model to build, improve, and run fuzzers itself instead of being limited to pure code auditing), to lead to a growing share of bugs being discovered by agentic systems.
Title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines

Text:
Project Zero often works with software vendors to remediate the vulnerabilities we report and provide broader guidance on making software more secure. Some vendors express concern about potential scenarios in which they are unable to fix vulnerabilities that are causing immediate user harm, due to limitations in their patch delivery systems. Since Project Zero encounters a wide array of systems designed to protect users in the case of exceptional exploitation scenarios, both through vendor discussions and security reviews, we want to share what we’ve learned.

This post provides an overview of systems in use by large vendors that allow them to remediate small volumes of vulnerabilities much faster than their typical update process. Our goal is to provide a reference for vendors seeking to implement or enhance the capabilities of such systems, and to encourage vendors to consider how they would fix an urgent vulnerability before they receive one.
Title: How to fix a bug in a fix

Text:
## Why patching takes time

Patching a vulnerability typically involves the following stages:

- Triage — a vulnerability report is received, validated, prioritized and assigned to a specific developer to be fixed
- Patch development — a software development team writes, reviews and commits code that fixes the vulnerability
- Testing — the patch is tested to ensure the vulnerability is remediated and the software still functions correctly when the patch is applied. This can include formal testing by a test team, automated testing and alpha and beta testing where a patch is shipped to a limited group of users for feedback on normal use.
- Partner review — some software updates require review by third parties before they can be shipped, due to relationships between the software vendor and other organizations, for example, carrier acceptance for some mobile updates.
- Delivery — the patch is delivered to and installed by end users
- Activation — sometimes an additional step, such as a system restart, is needed to switch the system to the updated software

Of course, this is a simplified picture. Patching can involve repeating steps, for example rewriting a patch if tests fail, or additional stages when third-party vendors are involved. However, this is a minimal set of steps most software updates require.
Title: How to fix a bug in a fix

Text:
## The challenges of emergency patches

While triage and patch development time contribute substantially to the speed at which vendors can generally patch vulnerabilities, they contribute less to emergency patch time. Triage is usually very fast in situations where vendors know they have an urgent problem, and patch development can be expedited based on priority. Only in rare circumstances, where a vulnerability is especially complex, or a vendor’s security team does not have a complete picture of their software’s components and who within their organization maintains them, have we seen urgent patches delayed in the triage or development phase. Likewise, partner agreements usually have exceptions for updates in emergency situations.

Most vendors’ patch speed is limited by the testing and delivery stages. Testing is important because all changes to software risk introducing unexpected behavior. The worst-case scenario is that inadequately tested software ‘bricks’ a device, causing it to malfunction in a way that it can no longer perform key functionality or receive software updates to remediate this. Buggy software updates have also led to situations where user data is corrupted or lost, and any decrease in software functionality after a security update makes users less likely to apply updates in the future.

The potential cost to vendors of shipping poorly tested updates varies depending on the nature of the underlying software. For example, if a mobile application is rendered unusable due to an update that corrupts local data or prevents it from launching, users can easily install the next version via an app store, and their data is usually saved on a remote server, so costs are limited to user support. Meanwhile, if a mobile device gets bricked, it needs to be returned to its manufacturer or place of purchase for repair, leading to substantial costs for the vendor and potentially the user.

The possibility of serious functional bugs is considered in the design of most patch delivery systems. Updates are often rolled out slowly, so that serious problems can be detected before they affect too many users. Often, patching vulnerabilities quickly and avoiding buggy patches are at odds with each other, requiring tradeoffs that prioritize one over the other.
Title: How to fix a bug in a fix

Text:
## The challenges of emergency patches

A variety of other technical challenges can limit the speed of patch delivery. One is the design of the patching system. A common design is that devices probe for updates at a regular interval, leading to patch saturation being limited to that interval. ‘Push’ style update systems can deliver patches to all users faster, but generally require more infrastructure.

User behavior and environment can also be a barrier to patch propagation. Patches that require user interaction to install are often delayed by users, and network speed and data cost are also factors in installation rate. Updating many users at once, as opposed to over a period of time, can strain patch delivery infrastructure. Chrome and Microsoft [have](https://blog.google/security/chrome-stronger-with-every-update/) [written](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/windows-itpro-blog/securing-devices-faster-with-hotpatch-updates-on-by-default/4500066) about the challenges of updates requiring restart to install, as users are often reluctant to restart their system and restarts take time.

While testing delays and limitations of the patch delivery system affect all updates, the shorter time frame of emergency updates make them a larger contributor to the overall time it takes to deliver a patch.

### Feature flags

Feature flags are conditional statements in source with paths determined by values provided by a remote server. They are often used for A/B testing, but they can also be used for short term remediation of vulnerabilities in emergency situations. A widely publicized case of this was a serious 2019 FaceTime [vulnerability](https://www.npr.org/2019/01/29/689581417/apple-disables-group-facetime-after-security-flaw-let-callers-secretly-eavesdrop), where Apple temporarily disabled Group Facetime with a feature flag. Several vendors have made at least some media codecs available in 0-click contexts controllable via feature flags, and can disable them in the case of active exploitation, falling back to another codec for realtime transmission.

The main benefit of feature flags as a vulnerability remediation method is that testing can be performed with each flag set in advance, so a fast update does not require shipping untested code. They can also be delivered to users much more quickly, as updating feature flags requires transmitting a very small amount of data.
Title: How to fix a bug in a fix

Text:
### Feature flags

Recently, Meta published a [blog post](https://engineering.fb.com/2026/04/09/developer-tools/escaping-the-fork-how-meta-modernized-webrtc-across-50-use-cases/) on how they implemented a ‘dual stack’ library, in which two versions of the WebRTC video conferencing library were compiled into a single binary, with the version in use controllable via a feature flag. This technology enables rapid updates with less testing, as new versions can be shipped with the option to quickly move users back to the previous version if function problems occur. While Meta uses two versions of the same library, it would also be possible to create a ‘dual stack’ with two different libraries that implement the same features (for example, two H264 libraries), allowing an application to switch to a different library to render a specific vulnerability unreachable without loss of functionality in an emergency. This would require additional testing, but it is testing that can be performed up front. It could also be possible to have a second library that enables performance intensive mitigations that would block many possible bugs, such as ASAN, or enabling DCHECKs.

### Filtering

Filtering is running a dynamically updatable ruleset, such as a regular expression, against untrusted input in order to block specific input that is required to reach a vulnerability. An example of this is Android’s [Intent Firewall](https://carteryagemann.com/pages/android-intent-firewall.html), which allows specific usages of an Android IPC mechanism called intents to be disabled based on rules in a dynamically updateable XML file, which enables blocking intents that can be used to exercise specific vulnerabilities. It was [recently used](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/09/intent-redirection-vulnerability-third-party-sdk-android/) to block vulnerabilities in third-party Android wallets.
Title: How to fix a bug in a fix

Text:
### Filtering

Some platforms have endpoint detection software that can perform filtering on a wide variety of system input, for example [Microsoft Defender](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/comprehensive-security) on Windows systems, and [Google Play Protect](https://developers.google.com/android/play-protect) on Android devices. Rules that block specific exploits or make certain vulnerabilities unreachable can often be deployed to these applications very quickly. Endpoint detection requires parsing a great deal of untrusted input, often in privileged context, so these applications are not without risk, but in systems where they already exist, they are a potential method of emergency remediation.

As an approach, filtering is more flexible than feature flags. For feature flags to be effective, the vendor needs to determine what features they might want to disable in advance, and if this isn’t comprehensive, they might find themselves in a situation where a vulnerability can’t be remediated via feature flags. Meanwhile, filtering can be used to block a wide variety of inputs, even ones that have never been considered. The downside of filtering is that performing filtering frequently can decrease software performance, and at least some testing of new filters is required, and can’t be performed upfront without knowing the vulnerability that needs to be blocked, as it is possible to write filters that interfere with necessary system functions.

### Alternate Channels

The network ‘channels’ used to deliver software updates to users can be slow for a variety of reasons discussed above. Vendors sometimes implement alternate channels that can be used to deliver smaller updates more quickly.

[Android Pony Express](https://source.android.com/docs/core/ota/apex) (APEX) is an example of an alternate channel that can be used to ship updates to specific high-risk Android components faster than a full system update. It shortens the patch development time, as OEMs do not need to integrate updates to APEX components. APEX is available to OEMs, and can be used to update OEM-maintained libraries.
Title: How to fix a bug in a fix

Text:
### Alternate Channels

Several applications we’ve researched have the ability to update individual libraries outside regular updates, usually by having some flag that is regularly checked over the network, and then downloading the library and loading it with `dlopen` or equivalent. While this is an effective way to avoid delivery-speed limitations of updates, it can also introduce critical vulnerabilities if libraries delivered in this way are not adequately verified by the client to have originated from the vendor. We encourage vendors to be cautious, and ensure that emergency update mechanisms of this variety have adequate security testing.

### Hotpatching

Some vendors have implemented update mechanisms that allow units of binary code smaller than libraries to be delivered and applied directly to the memory space of a running process. For example Linux supports [Livepatch](https://docs.kernel.org/livepatch/livepatch.html) which enables kernel functions to be directly replaced in memory without a restart. Similarly, Windows’ [hotpatch](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/get-started/hotpatch) allows security updates that contain only updated functions to be delivered to users, and applied while the process is still running.

Hotpatching has the potential to deliver very flexible security patches to software very quickly, with no degradation of user experience, though it typically has some limits to the nature of patches it can deliver, for example, updates that require changing the definition of a structure shared between functions are sometimes not supported. Hotpatching has similar security downsides to alternate channels, and also carries the risk of introducing ways to bypass exploit mitigations, as it requires permissions to map pages with write-execute privileges at some point during patching. It also doesn’t address any of the testing challenges of rapid updates, just the delivery challenges.
Title: How to fix a bug in a fix

Text:
## The importance of emergency patching

LLMs are increasing the vulnerability discovery and exploitation capabilities of both attackers and defenders. A wider array of actors now have the ability to perform novel attacks at greater speed. In light of this, it is important for vendors to consider how to protect their users in the case of active exploitation. Rapid update mechanisms do not need to be heavyweight or be capable of fixing every possible bug and preserving perfect user experience in every scenario. Technologies like feature flags, filtering and alternate update mechanisms can remediate the most likely and severe vulnerabilities in the short term, while keeping devices reasonably functional for users.

It is urgent for vendors to plan how they will protect their users in the worst case scenario of widespread active exploitation. Actions taken now can greatly improve security outcomes for users. By taking stock of update mechanisms already available to them and implementing rapid remediation functionality where gaps exist, vendors can be better prepared for whatever the future holds.
Title: How to fix a bug in a fix

Text:
This short blog post is about abusing a privilege escalation bug that Microsoft recently fixed in Windows, [CVE-2026-66804](https://project-zero.issues.chromium.org/issues/538151139), that I and 14 others reported. This issue is an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-50343, a bug dubbed “Dark Elevator” [by Calif](https://github.com/califio/publications/blob/main/MADBugs/windows-CVE-2026-50343/blog.md).

The root cause of the bug was a dangling COM object registration for the CrossDevice COM object with the CLSID `{E9F83CF2-E0C0-4CA7-AF01-E90C70BEF496}`. A COM registration typically needs two parts: a server executable, which for in-process components is a DLL and a CLSID entry under the `HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT` registry key which points to that DLL.

This object was registered in the system wide classes key, meaning it was accessible to all users on the system, including system services. However the server executable was missing. Specifically it was registered to use the DLL `%PROGRAMDATA%\CrossDevice\CrossDevice.Streaming.Source.dll`. Not only does this path not exist, it’s also within the `C:\ProgramData` directory. This is a [common location](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/shell/csidl#:~:text=FOLDERID_ProgramData) for all users on the system and therefore permits anyone to create directories. Therefore you can create an arbitrary DLL file at that location and the COM object can be instantiated potentially leading to privilege escalation.

But how to get the COM object, and thus the DLL, loaded into a privileged process? The fixed bug Calif blogged about, CVE-2026-50343, abused a weak registry key permissions to add the class as a installer plugin and then get the `InstallService` to load it into memory. The issue with the InstallService was fixed, so we need an alternative way to abuse the unfixed dangling COM reference.
Title: Windows Exploitation Techniques: Dangling COM Object Registrations

Text:
### Abuse Custom COM Marshaling, Again

A technique I’ve used multiple times in the past to load an arbitrary DLL into a privileged process is to abuse custom COM marshaling. When you call an interface method which is implemented out-of-process, the COM runtime will marshal the parameters into an RPC call to send to the server. If a parameter is a COM object then the runtime marshals that object into an OBJREF structure that allows the object to be used in the server. The two main types of OBJREFs are shown in the diagram below, or you can read about them in the official DCOM documentation [here](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/openspecs/windows_protocols/ms-dcom/fe6c5e46-adf8-4e34-a8de-3f756c875f31):

The default COM marshaling strategy is by reference which produces a Standard OBJREF containing all the information needed to connect to the original object. The object might even be on a completely different computer. When the object is unmarshaled this information is used to create an RPC channel back to the caller so that the server can call methods on the object.

The runtime also supports an opt-in marshal by value mechanism if the object implements the [IMarshal](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/objidl/nn-objidl-imarshal) interface. This allows the object to specify an arbitrary CLSID to use as the unmarshaling object, which doesn’t have to be the same as the object being passed in. When the object is unmarshaled in the server the CLSID is used to lookup an in-process server DLL to load.

We need to find a privileged service to send the marshaled COM object to become an administrator. Unfortunately, finding such a service isn’t so simple. The fact that a custom marshaling object will cause an arbitrary DLL to be loaded into the process and code executed is a risky operation, especially across privilege boundaries. Therefore Microsoft implemented a mitigation which can be enabled to [disable custom marshaling](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/com/categorizing-dcom-proxies-and-stubs) in the process unless the class is explicitly opted in, or is one of a small number of trusted components such as classes in the runtime library.
Title: Windows Exploitation Techniques: Dangling COM Object Registrations

Text:
### Abuse Custom COM Marshaling, Again

Since Windows 8 this mitigation is implemented through two mechanisms, the first and original method is setting the `EOAC_NO_CUSTOM_MARSHAL` capabilities flag when calling [CoInitializeSecurity](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/combaseapi/nf-combaseapi-coinitializesecurity). The second, added to improve security in AppContainer sandboxes is set through the [IGlobalOptions::Set](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/objidl/nf-objidl-iglobaloptions-set) method and specifying the `COMGLB_UNMARSHALING_POLICY` property type. As we’re not trying to escape from a sandbox the only value of importance is `COMGLB_UNMARSHALING_POLICY_STRONG` which disables custom marshaling similar to the capabilities flag.

As the dangling COM object isn’t registered as a trusted marshaler this means we need to find a privileged COM server that doesn’t enable these mitigations. The easiest approach is to scan the processes at runtime. The capability flags are stored in the value `combase!gCapabilities` while the marshaling policy is stored in `combase!g_GLBOPT_UnmarshalingPolicy`.

Normally, when a COM object is hosted by a privileged service, it’s registered with the name of a system service that RPCSS will start automatically when the object class is requested. However, in this case as there’s no service,creating the object fails with a “Class not registered” error. In order to create the COM server, the service needs to already be running as the SYSTEM user before you call `CoCreateInstance`.

You can verify that the object is hosted in a privileged process with the `Get-ComProcess` command and checking the `CustomMarshalAllowed` property. Note this command is currently broken on Windows 11 25H2 due to changing structures that I’ve not had a chance to update, it still works on previous versions.

The COM object only has one unique interface, `ICreateObject`. Converting the interface proxy to IDL shows that it takes an `IUnknown` pointer as its second parameter. Therefore to exploit the dangling COM registration we can just pass the “fake” marshaled object to this parameter and get privileged code execution. I’ve attached an updated, fully working exploit of the bug to the original issue [here](https://project-zero.issues.chromium.org/538151139#attachment81832125).
Title: Windows Exploitation Techniques: Dangling COM Object Registrations

Text:
### Abuse Custom COM Marshaling, Again

It’s worth noting that while this exploitation technique makes it easy to exploit dangling COM registrations, it can also be used to exploit buggy COM class custom unmarshalers. Sometimes, just the act of loading a DLL into a process can cause a crash.

### Finding the Original Dangling COM Object Registration

This will print out any in-process COM class from the machine hive where `LoadLibrary` can’t find the DLL. It’s important to use `LoadLibrary` via the `Import-Win32Module` command as some of the COM registrations only specify the file name and you want to ensure these are resolved correctly according to the system path.

This script will find the dangling CrossDevice COM class on an unpatched system. Note, you’ll need to manually inspect the paths to see if a DLL can be planted at that location. You could make it smarter by checking if the path is in a directory that can be written to, or even test if an existing DLL can be modified, but that’s an exercise for the reader.
Title: Windows Exploitation Techniques: Dangling COM Object Registrations

Text:
### Abuse Custom COM Marshaling, Again

Therefore an obvious technique to exploit the dangling COM object registration is to send a Custom OBJREF to a privileged COM service specifying the CLSID of the dangling object. When unmarshaled, which happens automatically in the runtime before the target method is called, the malicious DLL will be loaded and we’d get privilege escalation. The following code shows how trivial it is to specify the dangling COM class in an `IMarshal` implementation:

```
class FakeMarshal : public IMarshal {
    // Inherited via IMarshal
    HRESULT GetUnmarshalClass(REFIID riid, void* pv, 
                              DWORD dwDestContext, void* pvDestContext, 
                              DWORD mshlflags, CLSID* pCid) override
    {
        return CLSIDFromString(L"{E9F83CF2-E0C0-4CA7-AF01-E90C70BEF496}", pCid);
    }
    // ...
};
```

However, I kept thinking there must be a COM service that runs as SYSTEM and doesn’t enable custom marshaling. After a bit of fiddling I found one, although there’s no doubt others. It turned out to be a [COM service I’ve researched](https://project-zero.issues.chromium.org/issues/42451931) and exploited before, the `Shell Create Object Handler` object. This is an interesting COM object, in that while it runs in a SYSTEM service, it’s not directly instantiable:

```
PS> $cls = Get-ComClass -Clsid 135fd325-45b7-4c30-89f8-4386961669f0
PS> $o = New-ComObject -Class $cls
Exception calling "CreateInstanceAsObject" with "3" argument(s): "Class not registered"

PS> $cls.AppIdEntry | Select Name, RunAs, IsService
Name                        RunAs               IsService
----                        -----               ---------
Shell Create Object Handler nt authority\system     False
```

Instead you have to start the privileged server via the `\Microsoft\Windows\Shell\CreateObjectTask` scheduled task. Fortunately this task can be started by normal users, which you can verify with my `Get-AccessibleScheduledTask` command:

```
PS> Get-AccessibleScheduledTask -Executable | 
         ? Name -Match Shell\\CreateObjectTask
TokenId  Access                     Name
-------  ------                     ----
77E3156D GenericExecute|GenericRead ...\Shell\CreateObjectTask
```

Of course just starting this task is not enough, you also need to create a global named event, `ShellCreateObjectTaskReadyEvent` otherwise the task will immediately exit and not export the COM service. A simple script to create an instance is shown below:

```
PS> $ev = New-NtEvent -Win32Path "Global\ShellCreateObjectTaskReadyEvent" -InitialState $false
PS> Start-ScheduledTask -TaskPath "\Microsoft\Windows\Shell\" -TaskName "CreateObjectTask"
PS> $ev.Wait()
PS> $o = New-ComObject -Clsid "135fd325-45b7-4c30-89f8-4386961669f0"
PS> $o
InterfaceName Iid
------------- ---
IUnknown      00000000-0000-0000-c000-000000000046
```

```
PS> $objref = Get-ComObjRef -Object $o
PS> $p = Get-ComProcess -ProcessId $objref.ProcessId
PS> $p | Select Name, User, CustomMarshalAllowed
Name    User                CustomMarshalAllowed
----    ----                --------------------
dllhost NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM                 True
```

At this point we have everything we need to exploit the dangling COM object, we’ve got a COM service running as SYSTEM with custom marshaling allowed. We can use the [CoGetInstanceFromIStorage](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/objbase/nf-objbase-cogetinstancefromistorage) API to create the object, passing the “fake” marshaled object as the `pstg` parameter. This object will get marshaled to the COM server process and then unmarshaled unconditionally during object activation. We do need to implement a fake `IStorage` interface to get it past the local API implementation, which isn’t that difficult but I thought I’d see if there’s an easier way. Let’s look at the supported interfaces:

```
PS> Get-ComInterface -Object $o

Name                 IID               HasProxy   HasTypeLib     
----                 ---               --------   ----------     
IUnknown             00000000-0000-... False      False          
IMarshal             00000003-0000-... False      False          
IMarshal2            000001cf-0000-... False      False          
ICreateObject        75121952-e0d0-... True       False

PS> Get-ComInterface -Name ICreateObject | ConvertTo-ComSourceCode -Parse
[
  object,
  uuid(75121952-E0D0-43E5-9380-1D80483ACF72),
]
interface ICreateObject : IUnknown {
    HRESULT Proc3([in] GUID* p0, [in] IUnknown* p1, 
                  [in] GUID* p2, [out, iid_is(p2)] IUnknown** p3);
}
```
